Before an Elmhurst house can close

Elmhurst requires a passed sump pump inspection and a purchased transfer stamp before a sale inside city limits can close, and those two steps control the timeline more than anything else. The city requires the inspection for every residential and commercial property prior to closing, with some exceptions for condo complexes. A sale of a house in Elmhurst therefore starts with a phone call to the city, well ahead of the contract date.

  • Book the sump pump inspection at least two weeks before closing, because same-week slots are rare.
  • Submit the transfer stamp application on the city's online portal.
  • Settle every city account: utilities, inspection fees, building permit fees, fines and parking tickets.
  • Have the signed sales contract, the deed and the state MyDec declaration ready before the stamp is issued.

Addresses in unincorporated Elmhurst, which include a letter in the street number such as 16W212, do not need the city sump inspection or the city stamp.

What to bring and who to call

A little preparation keeps the city side of the sale from dragging. Before you book anything, pull together the signed sales contract, a copy of the deed, the closing and move-out dates, the buyer's name and your forwarding address. Those are the items the stamp application asks for, and having them in one folder saves a second trip to the portal.

Call (630) 530-3030 for the inspection and 630-530-3117 or 3118 for the stamp. If the inspection fails, the repair has to be finished and the inspection rebooked, so ask the inspector what failed while they are on site. An as-is buyer does not change this: the city still wants a pass before stamps are issued.

If you owe the city anything, pay it first. Unpaid utilities, permit fees, fines and parking tickets all hold up the stamp.

What the sump pump inspection checks

The inspection checks that the pit has a cover and that only stormwater drains to it. Bathrooms, washers and utility sinks may not drain into a storm pit. If the pump discharges overland, it must drain toward the middle of the front or back of the lot and cannot reach a neighbor's yard, the city sidewalk or the parkway. If it drains underground, it must connect to the storm sewer and never the sanitary sewer, since a sanitary connection is illegal.

A passing result earns a certificate of compliance on site, and an approved inspection is good for six months. A failed inspection means repairing the problem and rebooking before stamps are issued, and the city will not accept a legal letter in place of a pass. Someone over 18 must be present, and inspection requests left on voicemail are not accepted. The number is (630) 530-3030. An inspection done through RJN does not count.

  • The pit needs a cover.
  • Only stormwater may drain to the pit.
  • Overland discharge must not reach neighbors, the sidewalk or the parkway.
  • Underground discharge must connect to the storm sewer.

How much is the transfer stamp?

For most sales, the stamp costs $1.50 per $1,000 of the sale price, rounded to the nearest thousand, and the seller is responsible for buying it. The city wants all information five business days before it issues the stamp. You apply through the online portal, and the application asks for the property address, owner and buyer names, closing and move-out dates, the full consideration and the seller's forwarding address.

Beginning January 1, 2026, exempt transfers also need a stamp. Examples include adding or removing a name after marriage or divorce, transfers to or from a trust, foreclosure or short sale, transfers with governmental bodies, and transfers with consideration under $100. The exempt stamp has a $30 administrative fee, and it requires a sump pump inspection if none was done in the last five years. A signed and notarized deed goes with the application.

City Hall's finance counter issues stamps Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., or the city can mail one if you attach a prepaid shipping label. Payment options are online by card or e-check, or in person by cash, check or card. Questions go to the finance department at 630-530-3117 or 3118.

Transfer tax refund

A refund is available in one situation. Under the Elmhurst Municipal Code, the payor of the tax can receive a refund if they previously owned and lived in an Elmhurst home and, within 180 days of that closing, buy and occupy a new residence in Elmhurst. The city posts a Transfer Stamp Refund Form on its transfer stamp page.

This suits local move-up and downsizing sellers, who sell one Elmhurst home and buy another. Keep proof of both closings and both periods of occupancy. If you plan to leave the city, no refund applies.

Final water reading and trash carts

Once your sump pump inspection is approved and the stamp form is in, the city pulls your current and forwarding address information and sets the final water reading itself. You do not call to schedule it. The reading happens on the day of closing, and the final bill goes to the forwarding address listed on the transfer stamp request.

Garbage, sewer and water share one bill, so there is nothing extra to arrange for those services. The trash and recycling carts belong with the address, so leave them for the buyer.

Elmhurst housing snapshot

Elmhurst is a western suburb in DuPage and Cook counties with 46,111 residents. Turnover is low, with nearly 92 percent of residents in the same house a year earlier, and most homes are owner-occupied.

Schools, transit and recording

Elmhurst Community Unit School District 205 serves most of the city, and its high school is York Community High School. Villa Park District 45, Salt Creek District 48 and Hillside District 93 serve other parts, feeding into DuPage High School District 88 or Proviso West.

The Metra Union Pacific West Line stops at the Elmhurst station, Pace buses run through town, and O'Hare is about 18 minutes away. Several homes were designed by Mies van der Rohe, Frank Lloyd Wright and Walter Burley Griffin, which can set a house apart in a listing. The city has tended to flood after large rainfalls and is working on mitigation, so expect buyers to ask about the basement and the sump.

Deeds go to the DuPage County Recorder or the Cook County Clerk. Cook prices a deed at $107 on its schedule effective April 1, 2024, with state transfer tax at .50 per $500 and county tax at .25 per $500.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a sump pump inspection to sell in Elmhurst?

Yes, for properties inside city limits. An approved inspection is required before the city issues transfer stamps, with some exceptions for condominium complexes. Schedule it at least two weeks before closing, since same-week openings are unlikely.

How long is an Elmhurst sump pump certificate valid?

An approved inspection is good for six months, and the certificate shows its expiration date. Bring it to the City Hall finance counter when you collect your transfer stamps.

What is the Elmhurst transfer stamp rate?

It is $1.50 per $1,000 of the sale price, rounded to the nearest thousand, for non-exempt sales. Exempt transfers carry a $30 administrative fee. The seller is responsible for buying the stamp.

Is Elmhurst's sump rule the same in unincorporated areas?

No. A sump inspection and city stamps do not apply to unincorporated Elmhurst addresses, which show a letter in the street number such as 16W212. Check your address before you book.

Who pays for the final water reading in Elmhurst?

The city schedules the reading for the day of closing once your inspection is approved and your stamp form is filed. Your final bill goes to the forwarding address you list. Garbage, water and sewer share one bill, so there is nothing extra to arrange.

Ways to sell a house in Lombard

Lombard sellers choose between a traditional listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale, and a cash purchase of the house as-is. The village, in DuPage County, runs permitting and code enforcement through its Community Development Department, and deeds are recorded by the DuPage County Recorder, so those two offices set most of the practical timeline.

The 2020 census counted 44,476 people in Lombard, and the mid-2025 estimate is 44,399.

Lombard's character and housing

Lombard began as Babcock's Grove, named for early settlers on the DuPage River, and took its present name from a Chicago developer who mapped the settlement in 1868. The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad arrived in 1848, and the village incorporated in 1869. The village calls itself the Lilac Village. A colonel's estate left to the village in 1927 became Lilacia Park, with some 200 varieties of lilac, and the Lilac Time festival and parade have run since 1930 into mid-May. A house near the park or the downtown station can use that identity in its listing description.

Rental housing is a big part of the market: 70.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the median home value is $335,700, and median gross rent is $1,948. There are 17,262 households averaging 2.48 people, and median household income is $100,362.

Commuting and trails

The commute is short at 25.6 minutes on average. The Metra Union Pacific West Line connects the village to Ogilvie Transportation Center and out to Elburn, and the I-88 and I-355 corridors and Illinois Routes 38, 53, 56 and 64 serve drivers. Pace buses use Yorktown Center as a hub, and the Illinois Prairie Path and Great Western Trail run through on former rail lines.

Mention the walk to the train, the trails and the park in your listing, because commuters and trail users are the buyers who value them most.

Assessed values and local development

The village's fiscal year 2024 financial report cites a 9.79 percent increase in equalized assessed valuation, with new construction adding $5.06 million. Redevelopment projects near Yorktown Center include Lilac Station, Yorktown Reserve and the Summit at Yorktown.

Assessed value is one input to property tax bills, so ask the DuPage County Treasurer and Supervisor of Assessments for your parcel's current numbers before you set a price.

Which Lombard schools do buyers ask about?

Lombard's public high schools belong to Glenbard Township High School District 87, shared with Glen Ellyn, and Glenbard East High School is in the village. Elementary and middle schools (kindergarten through grade 8) belong to Lombard School District 44 or DuPage School District 45, depending on the street.

Line up the elementary district for your address before the first showing, since it shapes which families look at the house.

Permits and code rules

The Building Division handles signs, fire, fill and grade, new buildings, additions, backyard chickens, accessory structures and alterations. Permits can be requested online through the village portal, fees are paid when the permit is ready for pickup, and some items such as residential driveways, fences and new roofs carry flat rates. The division's number is (630) 620-5750.

  • Fences and grading: a permit is required for all fences and for all grading.
  • Exterior upkeep: grass and weeds must stay under eight inches during the growing season, and litter must be cleared within seven days.
  • Vehicles: inactive vehicles must be garaged and RVs may not sit in the front yard from November 1 through March 31.
  • Rentals: owners who rent must supply heat at 68 degrees from September 15 through June 1.
  • Address numbers: they must be visible and legible from the street.

A walk-through for these items before listing can head off an inspector's note. Lombard is a non-home-rule municipality with a council-manager government, so check the village code for local rules before you assume a state rule is the only one.

Owners should also keep waste containers covered, keep items on the parkway only within 24 hours of scheduled pickup, and park vehicles on an approved hard surface, not on grass. Commercial-size trucks are barred from residential districts. Tidy these before photographs, since a neighbor's complaint can bring an inspection.

Landmarks along the rail line

Lombard's older core grew up around its railroad. Stops on the old Chicago Aurora and Elgin line once sat at Stewart Avenue, Main Street, Brewster Avenue and Westmore and Meyers Road. Cartoonist Harold Gray drew Little Orphan Annie in a restored Italianate house from 1881 on Main Street, and the Maple Street Chapel (1870) served as the first town hall and library. Landmarks like these give streets a recognizable identity that buyers notice.

Recording with the DuPage County Recorder

The DuPage County Recorder maintains the county's land records back to 1839, and recording is fee-funded. The fee for a deed (Document Class 1) is $86, which includes $10 for document storage, $21 for GIS, $1 for the real property fee and $18 for the Rental Housing Support Program. The Recorder's office number is 630-407-5400.

The state transfer tax in 35 ILCS 200/31-10 runs fifty cents per $500 block of declared value, and 35 ILCS 200/31-25 requires a declaration signed by at least one seller and one buyer. Collection of the tax runs through the recorder, and the statute phases out paper revenue stamps in favor of electronic stamps or other indicia. Ask your closing agent whether the village or county adds any local fee on your parcel.

Order of tasks before closing

Most delays in a Lombard sale come from a handful of items that can be settled in a week or two.

  1. Walk the house with the permit and code list above in hand, and fix or disclose anything an inspector might note.
  2. Find permit records for any fence, driveway, roof or alteration, since the Building Division at (630) 620-5750 can tell you what is on file.
  3. Ask the DuPage County Treasurer about your current tax balance.
  4. Agree on a written closing date and who pays each recording item.
  5. Sign the state declaration, with a signature from at least one seller and one buyer, and send it with the deed to the DuPage County Recorder.

When does a cash sale suit a Lombard owner?

A cash sale suits owners who need to sell a house with deferred repairs, a tenant situation or an inherited estate without staging and showings. With median rent near $1,948, landlords holding an older Lombard rental sometimes prefer a clean exit over renovating. Ask any buyer for a written closing date and a list of who pays each recording item before you sign.

A cash sale also skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, so a deed that is ready to record is usually the only thing the timeline waits on.

Frequently asked questions

Which office records my deed in Lombard?

The DuPage County Recorder, whose records start in 1839. The deed fee includes storage, GIS, real property and Rental Housing Support Program amounts. Call 630-407-5400 for questions.

Is a fence permit required in Lombard?

Yes. Permits are required for all fences so the homeowner knows the requirements before buying the fence. Fences are among the flat-rate permits.

Can I park an RV in my front yard in winter?

No. RVs are not permitted in the front yard from November 1 through March 31, and vehicles that are not street ready must be garaged.

Which high school serves Lombard?

Glenbard East High School in Lombard belongs to Glenbard Township High School District 87. Elementary students attend Lombard School District 44 or DuPage School District 45 depending on the street.

What is the Illinois transfer tax rate?

The statute at 35 ILCS 200/31-10 sets it, counted in $500 units of the value on the declaration. A mortgage that stays on the property is left out of the base.

How owners usually sell in Buffalo Grove

Most Buffalo Grove owners list with an agent, because the housing market is built around mortgage-financed buyers and long-tenured owners. A direct sale to a cash buyer is the alternative when a house needs work or the closing date matters more than the top price.

The village adds one local step to every route. It sells its own real estate transfer stamps, in person only, and holds them back if water or other village debts are unpaid. Plan for the stamp early and it will not delay your closing.

  • Agent listing: more showings, more time, and the buyer's financing to wait on.
  • Owner sale: saves the commission, but you handle disclosures, the deed and the stamp visit.
  • Cash purchase: fewer contingencies and a closing date you set, usually at a lower price than a retail sale.

Cook County or Lake County?

Lake Cook Road splits the village. The northern part, about three-quarters of Buffalo Grove, is in Vernon Township in Lake County, and the southern part is in Wheeling Township in Cook County. Anyone changing the property record with Cook or Lake County needs a village stamp.

The deed is recorded with the Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division or with Lake County, depending on the parcel. Cook County Clerk's recordings hours run 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the last customer is accepted at 4:45 p.m. Property tax bills, exemptions and appeals follow the county, so find out which assessor and treasurer cover your parcel.

Transfer stamp cost and requirements

The village charges $3 per $1,000 for its transfer tax and will not issue a stamp while water, fines, fees or other debts to the village are outstanding. Stamps are sold only in person at Village Hall, 50 Raupp Boulevard.

Water and sewer balances

Water and sewer balances must be paid before the village issues a stamp, so settle the final bill ahead of closing. Rates as of January 2026 are $7.14 per 1,000 gallons for water and $1.77 per 1,000 gallons for sewer, a combined $8.91.

Houses on the Lake County side also pay a sanitary sewer pass-through fee of $5.26 per 1,000 gallons as of December 2025. That line shows on a Lake County bill and not on a Cook County neighbor's across Lake Cook Road.

The property check from the Finance Department is the fastest way to learn what you owe. Ask for the figure a few days before the closing date, then ask again if the date moves.

Pricing in an established village

The median owner-occupied home value is $412,300, and 79.8 percent of housing units are lived in by their owners. The 2020 count was 43,212 and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 42,812, down 0.9 percent. Median gross rent is $2,037, median household income is $129,395 for 2020 through 2024, and 88.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

Population has been flat for years. Pricing against recent sales on your own street matters more than the village-wide median, which blends very different subdivisions. Most of the village was platted after the 1950s, so a buyer's inspector will compare your house with others of the same era.

State rules behind the village stamp

Illinois imposes its own transfer tax at 50 cents per $500 of value, collected by the county recorder, and counties may add 25 cents per $500. Home rule municipalities such as Buffalo Grove can layer their own tax on top, which is why the village stamp exists.

Buyer and seller also complete the Illinois PTAX-203 transfer declaration, filed with the county where the property sits. Paper revenue stamps were scheduled for phase-out by December 31, 2025, after which counties issue electronic stamps. The village's own stamp is still issued in person.

Library districts and services

The split between counties also shows up in services. The Indian Trails Public Library District serves the Cook County part, and the Vernon Area Public Library District serves most of the Lake County part. Mention the right one in your listing so buyers know what to expect.

Flooding and drainage

Buffalo Grove uses open space for flood control. Buffalo Creek forest preserve works as flood control, and the Buffalo Grove Golf Course is used as a floodplain. Buyers near those areas ask about basement dampness and drainage.

Gather sump pump service records and permits for any roof or foundation work. Those papers answer the questions before a buyer has to raise them.

Selling when the house needs work

A house with deferred repairs can still sell. Retail buyers who need a mortgage often ask for repairs or credits after their inspection, and a lender may balk at certain conditions. A cash buyer takes the house as it stands, so the sale depends less on what an appraisal or an inspection finds.

The trade-off is price. A cash offer usually lands below what a fully updated house could bring, so weigh the offer against the repair bill, the months of carrying costs while the house sits, and the date you need to close. The village steps are the same for each route, so they should not tip the choice either way.

Putting the sale in order

A typical sequence runs like this. Order a property check from Finance and pay any balance. Schedule the final water reading. Fill out the village form with your buyer, and complete the PTAX-203 or MyDec form. Visit Village Hall with the deed or latest tax bill, the closing date and your forwarding address. Take the stamp to closing so the county can record the deed.

A cash buyer can run the same list in less time because no lender is waiting on paperwork. A listing buyer's lender may set its own deadlines, so ask the title company which dates are fixed.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Buffalo Grove transfer tax?

The village charges $3 per $1,000. You also give the closing date and a forwarding address when you buy the stamp.

Can I get a Buffalo Grove transfer stamp online?

No. Stamps are issued only in person at Village Hall, 50 Raupp Boulevard, after a property check with the Finance Department at 847-459-2500.

What blocks a stamp from being issued?

Delinquent water charges, outstanding fines or fees, or any other debt owed to the village. All debts must be paid before even an exempt stamp is issued.

Is Buffalo Grove in Cook County or Lake County?

Both. Lake Cook Road divides the village, with about three-quarters in Lake County's Vernon Township and the rest in Cook County's Wheeling Township. Your parcel determines where the deed is recorded.

Do I need a deed to get the stamp?

You need the deed or the most recent tax bill for the property. If you lack the deed, the Cook County Clerk or Lake County recording office can supply a copy.

Ways to sell quickly in Moline

Moline owners have three choices: an agent, a buyer found without one, or a purchaser who pays cash and takes the house as found. That last choice closes soonest, with an offer shaped by the work needed.

Moline is a Quad Cities city, and the buyers who show up here are shaped by that. Some are workers tied to the large employers along the river, some are investors, and some are families moving within the Illinois and Iowa sides of the metro. Knowing which group your house suits helps you choose the route.

What follows is local: housing figures, neighborhoods and school boundaries, the city's building office, and the filing rules at the Rock Island County Recorder.

Moline housing figures

Moline counted 42,985 people in 2020 and an estimated 42,362 in July 2025, a dip of 1.4 percent. The median owned home is valued at $146,300 and median rent is $900 (2020 to 2024). Owners live in 67.3 percent of homes, across 18,289 households of about 2.29 people. Household income at the median is $67,701, and the average drive to work is just 18.0 minutes.

  • At these prices a repair bill takes a larger bite of the sale price, so get quotes before you decide to renovate.
  • A short commute and a large employment base make renting out a house a realistic option for some owners, and buyers who rent houses out may bid on yours.
  • The estimate has slipped a little since 2020, so buyers can be choosy, and a house needing work may wait longer on the open market.

Neighborhoods and school districts

Moline sits on a bluff between the Mississippi and Rock rivers, and deep ravines cut the high ground into natural neighborhoods. Neighborhood associations work with the city, and the downtown area is known as Moline Centre. Other neighborhood names in common use include Floreciente, Olde Towne, Uptown, Overlook, Wharton, Hamilton Heights, Prospect Park, Park Hill, Forest Hill and Highland. A listing that names the neighborhood reads more clearly to local buyers than a street address alone.

Moline School District No. 40 covers most of the city, with about 7,500 students in twelve elementary schools, two middle schools named for John Deere and Woodrow Wilson, and Moline High School. Pieces of the city on the east side belong to East Moline District 37 and United Township High School District 30, and a southwest piece belongs to Rock Island-Milan District 41. Verify the district for an address before you advertise one.

Roads and employers

Interstate 74 runs straight through the city and splits it into two roughly equal halves, and Interstate 280 circles the Quad Cities. Moline is about 165 miles west of Chicago.

Deere and Company keeps its corporate headquarters in Moline, and Kone's U.S. division is based in the city as well. Black Hawk College and the Quad Cities campus of Western Illinois University are both in Moline, and Quad Cities International Airport sits on the south edge of town. South Park Mall and a string of big-box centers make the city a retail hub.

The downtown arena, Vibrant Arena at The MARK, and John Deere Commons draw events that fill nearby restaurants and hotels. Houses within a short drive of these destinations tend to be pitched to commuters and renters, so say so in your listing.

Winter wear and what buyers inspect

Moline sees 43 days a year when the high never climbs above freezing and 31.6 inches of snow a season, and summers run hot and humid. Buyers will check the roof, the furnace and the air conditioner, because a house here works both systems hard. The freeze-thaw cycle also tests sidewalks, driveways and foundation walls.

Houses on bluffs and ravine edges also deserve a look at drainage and grading. If a lot slopes toward the foundation, expect an inspector to flag it.

City permits and code questions

The Building and Inspections Division is at the City Services Center, 1830 6th Avenue, and visitors use the north entrance on 6th Avenue. It handles building permits and plan reviews, building inspections, contractor registration, food establishment licensing and code enforcement.

Code complaints about housing, nuisance, vegetation, zoning and signs go through the City's Neighborhood Improvement Officer, who also works with the neighborhood groups. If your house has an open complaint or a citation, resolve it or ask the city what a closing needs, because a title company can discover it.

  • Pull permit records for any remodel, deck, roof or mechanical work done in your years of ownership.
  • Ask the division how to close out any permit that was opened but never finished.
  • Ask the water and sewer divisions about final billing before the closing date.

The city publishes its Code of Ordinances online for anyone who wants to check a rule before listing.

How a Moline deed gets recorded

Recording for a Moline address takes place in neighboring Rock Island, at the Recorder's second-floor office at 1504 3rd Avenue (309-558-3360). Counter hours are weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The county lays out format rules: white letter-size paper, a clear 3 by 5 inch box at the top right of page one, no staples or tape, black ink and type of at least 10 points. The document must name its preparer and a return address, and a deed adds the grantee's address and a spot for the tax bill mailing address.

Under 35 ILCS 200/31-15 the state charges fifty cents for every $500 of value. Call the Recorder to ask whether a county or city stamp is added.

What a Moline seller should have ready before an offer

Start with the disclosure report. State law, 765 ILCS 77/20, has the seller complete each item and hand the report over ahead of the signed contract.

Then pull together the closing file: parcel number, newest tax bill, any loan payoff figure and the permit history. A rented house also needs its leases and tenant contacts, which a buyer will want to read.

Weigh at least two offers by what you would net, not by the headline figure. Ask each buyer who covers transfer stamps, which repairs they expect and how fast they can close.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, which is why a cash sale tends to close soonest. The deed still has to meet the county's format rules, so check the checklist above before you sign.

Do houses sell quickly in Moline?

It varies. The median home value of $146,300 is modest, and the population estimate has eased since 2020, so a house needing repairs may linger on the market. A purchase by a cash buyer is usually the quickest way out.

Which office files a Moline deed?

The Rock Island County Recorder, whose second-floor counter at 1504 3rd Avenue opens weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call 309-558-3360.

What formatting does Rock Island County insist on for deeds?

Letter-size white paper, an empty 3 by 5 inch area in the upper right of page one, black ink at 10 points or larger, nothing attached, and lines naming the preparer and where to send the document back. Deeds also carry the grantee's address and the address for tax bills.

Who approves building work on a Moline house?

The city's Building and Inspections Division reviews plans, issues permits, runs inspections and registers contractors. Contact it at the City Services Center on 6th Avenue before starting a project.

What paperwork must a Moline seller give the buyer?

A finished residential disclosure report, in the buyer's hands before the contract is signed (765 ILCS 77/20). The state transfer tax, fifty cents per $500, is paid when the deed is recorded.

No city transfer tax in Crystal Lake

Crystal Lake charges no city transfer tax, and the McHenry County Recorder confirms that no municipality in the county charges its own. The state tax still applies.

The city sits about 45 miles northwest of Chicago and is the county's most populous city. Population is 42,288, up 5.0 percent from the 2020 count of 40,269. About 77.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, with a middle value of $311,400, and households earn a middle income of $108,418. The city has 14,806 households of about 2.72 people. This is an owner market with steady demand, so a house in good shape has real options beyond a cash sale.

The sale process step by step

A Crystal Lake sale follows the standard Illinois sequence, with only a few city-level touchpoints. You sign a contract, deliver the disclosure report, clear title, pay off any mortgage, sign the deed and have it recorded with the McHenry County Recorder.

Offices that touch a Crystal Lake home sale

A new deed is required to change ownership, and the Recorder suggests using an attorney. Deed forms are free at the office. The PTAX-203 or MyDec form filed with the deed shows the full consideration, which is the base for the state tax of fifty cents per $500 in Article 31 of the Property Tax Code.

Before you sign anything, gather your latest tax bill, your mortgage payoff figure, the permits you pulled and any warranty papers. At the closing table you sign the deed and the declaration, the title company pays off your lender and prorates the taxes, and the deed goes to the Recorder. Call Water Billing a few days ahead so the final reading lands on the closing date. With a cash buyer the same steps apply, but the appraisal and lender underwriting drop out, which is where most of the time savings come from.

City rules for sellers and buyers

Crystal Lake's rules are mostly about utilities, permits and streets. There is no point-of-sale inspection. City Hall stands at 100 W. Woodstock Street, with weekday hours of 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM and a main line of (815) 459-2020.

  • Permits: the Building Division issues building, electrical and plumbing permits and enforces the building, housing, pollution control and fire codes. If you started a project and did not finish it, call before you list.
  • Water and sewer: the buyer sets up service by contacting Water Billing, and the city offers a Direct Debit Program.
  • Garbage: the city's residential contractor is Lakeshore Recycling Systems, which provides weekly curbside collection and one bulk item per week.
  • Street parking: parking on city streets is prohibited from 2:00 AM to 6:00 AM year-round, which matters for open house guests.

Open permits and unfinished work tend to surface in inspection and title review, so closing them out before listing avoids a later argument.

Neighborhoods that shape value

Buyers sort Crystal Lake by neighborhood and school boundary more than by city name. Downtown surrounds Crystal Lake Central High School and has the widest range of house sizes and ages. Directly south is the Coventry neighborhood, and southwest of downtown is the sprawling Four Colonies area. South of that are The Villages, named for Village Road.

North of downtown, the area near Prairie Ridge High School has large houses on widely spaced lots, and Burtons Bridge sits at the northeast edge next to the Fox River.

Outdoor recreation helps listings. The separate Crystal Lake Park District runs more than 40 parks, including 140-acre Veteran Acres Park and 305-acre Lippold Park.

Schools and commuting

Crystal Lake buyers frequently commute, so schools and the Metra station are the first questions. Community High School District 155 runs the high schools, and Crystal Lake Community Consolidated School District 47 operates the elementary and middle schools. Part of the northeast side is served by Prairie Grove Consolidated School District 46.

The Metra Union Pacific Northwest Line runs to Chicago's Ogilvie Transportation Center, with stops at Crystal Lake and Pingree Road. U.S. Route 14, Illinois Route 176 and Illinois Route 31 serve the city by road, and O'Hare International Airport is about a 45-minute drive. Mention the train and the district in your listing or when you talk to a buyer, since both shape what a family will pay.

What an Illinois seller must disclose

Illinois law has the seller fill in a residential disclosure report and hand it over ahead of signing. The duty is in Section 20 of the disclosure Act, and Section 35 holds the form.

The report covers flood hazard insurance, flooding or recurring leakage in the basement or crawl space, whether the property is in a floodplain, and defects in the foundation, roof, walls, electrical, plumbing and heating systems. It also asks about wells, septic and sanitary sewer systems, radon, asbestos, lead, mine subsidence, termites, underground fuel tanks and boundary disputes. The form requires an explanation for any answer of yes or not applicable, except on the first question.

Answers rest on what you actually know, with no special investigation required. The form is a disclosure rather than a warranty and leaves room for a buyer's own inspection.

Cash offer or market listing

Condition, deadline and appetite for effort decide it. Cash makes sense for a house needing repairs, a firm move-out date or a wish to skip showings, and a listing suits a house that is ready to show.

  • List the repairs a buyer's inspector would flag and get bids for them.
  • Add the cost of carrying the home while it is listed, including taxes, utilities and insurance.
  • Ask what closing date the buyer will commit to in writing.
  • Confirm any open permits are closed or that the buyer accepts them.

Tax bill information is on the McHenry County Treasurer's site. Ask the title company to show the prorated tax lines on your settlement statement, and keep your latest bill handy.

If the house is not ready to show, ask a cash buyer to put the offer in writing with the closing date, who pays title and recording charges, and what happens if the inspection turns up something new. Then set that figure next to the net from a listing after repairs, carrying costs and commission. The better choice is the one that leaves more in your pocket by the date you need to move.

Frequently asked questions

Does Crystal Lake charge a transfer tax when I sell?

No city tax exists, and the McHenry County Recorder confirms that no municipality in the county levies one. The state tax still applies.

Is a city inspection required before a Crystal Lake sale?

No point-of-sale inspection is required. Call the Building Division at (815) 356-3605 to ask about open permits on the property.

Where is the deed recorded for a Crystal Lake property?

It is recorded with the McHenry County Recorder. A new deed is required to change ownership, and an attorney is recommended.

How do I end water service when I sell?

Contact the city's Water Billing office at (815) 459-2020. Ask about the final reading and how the closing date will be handled.

Can I sell my Crystal Lake house as-is?

Yes, provided the Illinois disclosure report reaches the buyer first. The form itself recognizes that parties may agree to an as-is deal.

Quick-sale options in Romeoville

Romeoville sellers choose between a regular listing, a sale without an agent, and a direct sale to a buyer paying cash. The cash route shortens the timeline most. No matter which you pick, the village's clearance letter and transfer stamp apply to every sale, and the clearance letter expires after five business days, so time your request carefully.

  • A listing exposes the house to the most buyers and usually has the slowest closing.
  • A private sale avoids commission and leaves marketing and negotiation to you.
  • A direct sale to a cash buyer is typically as-is, with a closing date the seller sets.

Romeoville housing at a glance

Romeoville is a Will County village about 26 miles southwest of Chicago, between Bolingbrook and Joliet near Interstates 55 and 355. It has an estimated 41,281 residents, up 1.2% from 2020, and 13,296 households averaging 3.05 people. Ownership dominates: 80.7% of units are owner-occupied. The middle home value is $257,100, the middle gross rent is $1,886, and middle owner cost with a mortgage is $1,934 a month.

Much of the housing went up after the Weber Road interchange opened on I-55 in 1990, so many houses are younger than those in older inner suburbs. Buyers therefore tend to compare condition and finishes. Warehouse, refinery and retail jobs cluster near I-55, and a house with quick access to that interchange gives a buyer a shorter drive to work.

What must happen at the village before closing?

Romeoville's Real Estate Transfer Tax is the buyer's responsibility, but the seller has to clear the property first. To get a transfer stamp, the property must be free of debts to the village, including the most current water bill. You request a clearance letter, which starts the process and orders a final water reading. Letters are valid for five business days. An exempt transaction does not need a final meter reading if the water account is in good standing and the name stays the same.

Romeoville transfer tax
Transaction typeVillage charge
Nonexempt$3.50 per $1,000 of full consideration
Exempt$40 processing fee

You can pay online by credit card or e-check, or in person. After payment you receive a receipt with space for the stamp, and the physical stamp can be handed over or mailed. A lost stamp must be repurchased at full price.

A refund exists only for residents who sell the home they live in and buy another Romeoville home as a new principal residence, with the two deals within 12 months of each other. The Finance Department is at 1050 W Romeo Road, phone 815-886-7212.

Final water bill

The final water bill is part of the clearance. The village mails it to the forwarding address you give after closing. Your account stays in your name until a final on-site meter read is done, so give the Water Billing office your closing date and mailing address ahead of time.

Any unpaid balance blocks the stamp, and that in turn blocks recording. Paying the account in full the day the reading posts keeps the closing on schedule.

State and county stamps on the deed

State law sets the Illinois stamp at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction, sold through the county recorder (35 ILCS 200/31-15). A deed will not be accepted for filing until those stamps have been bought from the recorder of the county where it is filed (35 ILCS 200/31-20). Romeoville is in Will County, so the recording office there handles the filing. The county sets its own stamp amount and fee schedule, so ask the Will County Clerk's recording office for current figures.

Your title company normally prepares the state transfer declaration and delivers the deed with the village stamp attached.

How Will County property tax works for a seller

Will County mails bills on May 1 for the previous tax year. The first installment comes due in June and the second in September, and postmarks count. Late payments accrue interest under state statute, starting at 1.5% per month on the first installment from June 2, with the rate stepping up in later months.

As a seller, confirm that both installments are paid and settle the proration on the closing statement. The calendar changes yearly, so ask the Will County Treasurer for the schedule that fits your sale date.

Your Romeoville closing checklist

A sale here moves faster when you tackle the village steps in order. Plan on this sequence:

  • Once you have a signed contract, request the clearance letter close to the closing date, since it lasts only five business days.
  • Give Water Billing your closing date and forwarding address so the final read is booked.
  • Pay any outstanding village balance, including the water bill, so the stamp can be issued.
  • Ask your title company to prepare the state transfer declaration and collect the county stamp.
  • Confirm the buyer has paid the village transfer tax and that you receive the stamped receipt.
  • Check with the Will County Treasurer that both installments are settled.

A cash buyer does not have a lender's appraisal and underwriting to wait for, so these village steps are often the longest items left on the calendar. Starting them early is the simplest way to keep a quick closing quick.

Exempt sales and the $40 fee

Some transfers qualify as exempt from the village tax, and those carry the flat $40 processing fee instead of the per-$1,000 charge. The account still has to be in good standing, and the village still wants the clearance letter first. If the same name stays on the water account, no final meter reading is needed. If you think your transfer might be exempt, say so when you call the Finance Department so the right paperwork is prepared from the start. Ask the title company to confirm the exemption before anyone pays the wrong amount.

What a cash sale skips

A cash buyer typically takes the house as is, so you do not repaint, replace flooring or stage rooms. There is no lender appraisal, and the closing date is the one you set. The village paperwork does not disappear, though. The clearance letter, the water read, the stamp and the recorded deed all apply, so a cash sale saves you the lender's timeline and the repair negotiations, not the local steps.

If the house sits empty while you wait, keep the water account current and the property tidy. An open village balance is the most common thing that holds up a stamp.

Who pays the transfer tax in Romeoville?

The buyer is responsible for the village's Real Estate Transfer Tax. The seller still has to clear all village debts first, including the water bill.

How long is a Romeoville clearance letter good for?

Five business days. The letter starts the clearance process and orders the final water reading, so request it close to your closing date.

Do I need a final water reading when I sell in Romeoville?

Usually yes. An exempt transaction can skip it if the account is in good standing and the name stays the same. Otherwise your account stays open until a final on-site read, and the last bill goes to your forwarding address.

Can I get a transfer tax refund in Romeoville?

Only if you live in the home, sell it, and buy another Romeoville home as your new principal residence within 12 months. Owner-occupants who sell and buy outside the village do not qualify.

Which county records a Romeoville deed?

Will County. The deed goes to the Will County recording office with the state and county stamps and the village stamp. Your title company usually files it.

Bartlett and its three counties

Bartlett is a Chicago-area village split mostly between Cook and DuPage counties, with a small parcel at its western edge in Kane County. The 2020 count was 41,105 residents, and the July 2025 estimate of 40,855 is 0.7% lower.

Three counties mean three recorders and three tax offices. The first move in any Bartlett sale is reading the parcel number on your tax bill to learn which one applies.

The Bartlett housing stock

Most of the population growth came in the 1980s, so the housing is recent compared with the depot-era town center, where the original 1873 station still stands as the Bartlett Depot Museum. The village was incorporated on June 21, 1892. Of 14,522 housing units in the 2020 count, 2.2% were vacant, and the homeowner vacancy rate was 0.9%.

Bartlett leans toward owner-occupied family housing: about 89% of homes are owner-occupied, and 36.6% of households had children under 18 in 2020. That mix means buyers often ask about schools, yards and commute time, so have those answers ready.

Schools and roads

Public schools in Bartlett are entirely within Elgin Area School District U46, the second largest district in Illinois. Bartlett High School, Eastview Middle School and elementary schools named Bartlett, Centennial, Sycamore Trails, Prairieview, Nature Ridge and Liberty serve the village, and some students attend South Elgin High School or Kenyon Woods Middle School in South Elgin.

Illinois Route 59 is the main north-south road, with a large retail area at Route 59 and Stearns Road. The Milwaukee District West rail line stops at Bartlett station and runs east to Chicago Union Station, and Pace bus Route 554 connects the village to Elgin and Schaumburg. The mean commute is 29.7 minutes, so buyers who ride the train will ask how far a house is from the platform.

Permits and driveways

The village's Building Division issues permits for work from decks and pools to driveways and new construction, and inspections by building staff run Monday through Friday only. You can reach the division at 630.540.5920.

The village's rules on new driveways are specific and worth reading before you list a house with a worn drive.

  • The apron, the part of the driveway that meets the street, is the homeowner's responsibility, and the village does not maintain or replace it.
  • Public works inspects the public sidewalk and utilities inside the driveway during permit review. If the sidewalk needs repair the village will do it, which can take up to four weeks and delay the permit.
  • No apron extension is approved when a parkway tree stands within 10 feet of it, and the village will not remove parkway trees for that purpose.
  • If a concrete contractor repairs the public sidewalk, Public Works will reimburse part of the cost. Call 630-837-0811.

Sprinklers and invisible fences placed in the village right-of-way are also the homeowner's problem if sidewalk work damages them. Ask the Building Division for the permit record on your address, and close out any open permit before a buyer's inspector finds it.

Deed, transfer declaration and recording

County recorders sell the revenue stamps that pay the Illinois transfer tax. Home rule municipalities may add their own tax, so ask the title company whether the village charges one.

The PTAX-203 declaration goes to the county of the parcel. In Cook County the Clerk's deed fee is $107 on the schedule that began April 1, 2024, a sum covering recording, GIS, storage, the state rental housing support fee and a filer fee. Parcels in DuPage or Kane have their own fee lists, so call that recorder.

Ask the title company early which recorder will file your deed, and keep the recorded deed and your copy of the transfer declaration once the county returns them.

Is a cash sale worth considering?

A tidy house can go through a regular listing. A cash offer suits a house needing major work, a move on a deadline, or an estate. The trade is speed and certainty against the higher price a fully updated listing might bring.

  • Get the offer in writing and see who pays closing costs.
  • Name the title company early and learn which recorder will file the deed.
  • Hold on to the recorded deed and your copy of the transfer declaration.

Whichever route you choose, line up the same set of papers: the parcel number, your latest tax bill, any payoff letter from a lender, and the permit record from the Building Division. A buyer who sees those up front tends to close with fewer questions.

How a Bartlett closing moves

Once a contract is signed, the title company orders the search and works out the tax proration for the year. Because the village crosses county lines, the first call is to the recorder that matches your parcel. The seller's side signs the deed and the transfer declaration, the lender, if any, issues a payoff, and the recorder files the deed. Plan for the Building Division to close any open permit before that date, since a permit problem can hold up a buyer's financing or inspection. If the house has a worn driveway apron or a cracked public sidewalk, raise it early and ask Public Works about the reimbursement above rather than leaving it for the buyer.

What to have ready for the title company

Gather the documents a buyer and title company ask for before the contract is even signed. That means your parcel number, the latest tax bill showing the county, any mortgage payoff information, and the permit record for the address. If you finished a basement, built a deck or replaced a driveway, find the permit paperwork and the final inspection, since unfinished items are the ones that surprise buyers.

Ask the title company who pays for the title search and recording, and put the answer in the contract. If you are selling for cash, ask for the offer in writing and compare it with what a listing would net after repairs and fees. If the house is vacant, say so up front, because buyers price in the cost of getting a vacant property ready. A written timeline for closing day, including what happens to utilities and keys, helps both sides avoid confusion.

Frequently asked questions

Which county holds my Bartlett parcel?

Read the parcel number on your tax bill. Bartlett is mostly in Cook and DuPage counties, plus a small piece of Kane. That county's recorder files the deed and its treasurer collects the tax.

What does a deed filing cost at the Cook County Clerk?

$107 on the schedule effective April 1, 2024. It rolls together the county recording fee, a GIS fee, a storage fee, the state rental housing support fee and a filer fee. DuPage and Kane parcels follow those counties' fees.

Is a permit required for a new driveway?

Yes. The Building Division issues driveway permits, and public works reviews the sidewalk and utilities inside the driveway. Sidewalk repair can take up to four weeks and hold up the permit, so apply early and call 630.540.5920.

Who runs the schools in Bartlett?

Elgin Area School District U46, the second largest in Illinois, serves the entire village. Some students attend South Elgin High School instead of Bartlett High School.

May I sell in as-is condition?

Yes, either to a cash buyer or through a listing priced for the condition. Pull your permit record first so nothing surprises the buyer.

Ways to sell quickly in DeKalb

Cash from a purchaser who takes the property exactly as it stands usually closes fastest, because no bank appraisal or repair list stands in the way. Hiring a broker or going it alone can also succeed, though both wait on showings, inspections and a buyer's mortgage approval.

  • A broker fits a sound house and an owner with time to spare.
  • Going private fits a seller who is at ease with contracts, disclosure forms and setting a price.
  • A straight cash sale fits probate homes, occupied rentals, neglected properties and owners racing a moving date.

DeKalb draws an unusually mixed set of purchasers. A university town with warehouses near the interstates attracts owner-occupants, landlords and investors alike.

DeKalb housing numbers

DeKalb has 40,467 residents, and renters outnumber owners. Northern Illinois University, with about 20,000 students, is the largest employer, which keeps a steady pool of rental demand. The median age is just 27.7. Of 16,629 housing units, 8.2 percent stand vacant.

DeKalb housing figures, 2020 to 2024
MeasureDeKalb
Middle value of homes their owners occupy$204,700
Owner-occupied share of housing units42.1%
Median gross monthly rent$1,029

With owners living in just 42.1 percent of units, a large part of the stock is rental. An investor buyer will likely want copies of leases, a rent roll and proof of city registration.

Pricing a DeKalb house means looking at both groups of buyers. A family buying to live in it cares about the roof, the basement and the school district. An investor cares about rent, vacancy and what the city will require. Ask any cash buyer how they arrived at their number, and ask for the closing date in writing.

Flood history and weather

An average year brings 37.25 inches of precipitation and 33.1 inches of snowfall, and the wettest months are May and June.

The Kishwaukee River crested at 15.27 feet on August 24, 2007 and flooded parts of town. If your house is near the river or has ever taken on basement water, say so up front and keep your repair receipts. Buyers' inspectors in this climate look first at roofs, gutters and sump pumps.

When you list or negotiate, keep the paperwork for any sump pump, drainage or waterproofing work. A buyer's inspector will look for water stains, and a folder of receipts answers the question before it becomes a price cut. The disclosure form asks about basement leakage and flooding in any case, so answer it from what you actually know.

DeKalb rental registration and property upkeep

Landlords must register each rental with the city every year. Chapter 10 of the municipal code, revised in October 2022, built the Crime Free Housing Program into that requirement.

  • Registration comes with a security plan aimed at preventing unlawful activity on the premises.
  • Each lease carries a crime free lease provision.
  • Owners attend a class once, then a refresher every year after that, and the city posts the refresher slides online.

Upkeep falls to the Building and Code Compliance Division at 164 East Lincoln Highway, reachable at 815-748-2070. Inspectors apply the International Property Maintenance Code through Chapter 24, mostly by viewing properties from public ground and answering complaints about weeds, trash, snow and ice, and inoperable cars. The city posts annual violation listings, so a seller can learn whether a parcel was cited before a buyer finds out.

Selling a rental? Ask the Crime Free Housing Bureau what your current registration status is and what the next owner has to file.

Recording a DeKalb deed

Deeds go to the DeKalb County Clerk and Recorder on the second floor of the Administration Building, 110 East Sycamore Street, Sycamore, open weekdays from 8:30 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon. Recording questions go to 815-895-7156. Title companies, attorneys and lenders can record electronically, and mailed or hand-carried paper still works.

The Recorder's fee schedule is $74.00 for a standard letter-size deed and $94.00 for a larger page. Transfer stamps are 50 cents per $500 of value for the State and 25 cents per $500 for the County, and the state declaration is filed through MyDec. A deed must show who prepared it, where to return it, where to send tax bills, the PIN and the street address.

DeKalb County tax bills

The Treasurer mails a single bill around May 1 with two coupons. Due dates land near June 1 and September 1 each year. Each month of delay adds 1.5 percent, and taxes still open after the second installment can be sold, with redemption handled by the County Clerk at 815-895-7149.

A buyer who receives a bill in a former owner's name can download a copy from the county's online portal, and a seller no longer holding title should pass the bill along. Treasurer's office: 815-895-7112.

Ask the title company to show how the current year's bill is split at closing. Since the bill arrives in May and is paid in two coupons, a sale in the second half of the year usually means the first coupon is already settled and the second is prorated between you and the buyer.

Selling a DeKalb house with tenants

Because renters outnumber owners here, many sellers have someone living in the house. Buyers who purchase occupied rentals usually want the same short list, so assemble it before you take calls:

  • Signed leases and any addenda, including the crime free lease provision.
  • A rent roll showing what each tenant pays and when.
  • Security deposit records, so the title company can credit the deposit to the buyer.
  • Proof that the rental registration with the city is current.
  • Tenant phone numbers, in case the buyer wants a walk-through.

Tell tenants about the sale in writing and keep access reasonable. A cash buyer will often take the house with the tenants in place, which spares you from a turnover, but the price will reflect the leases, the rents and the condition of the unit.

Paperwork a DeKalb seller should collect

A brief checklist keeps the closing on schedule.

  1. Find the PIN and street address that must appear on the deed.
  2. Download your newest bill from the Treasurer's portal.
  3. Ask the city about unresolved rental registration or violation notices.
  4. Assemble leases, deposit records and tenant phone numbers for an occupied house.
  5. Ask each lender or lienholder for a payoff letter.

Once a contract is signed, the title company searches the record, drafts the deed, files the state declaration and sends the deed to Sycamore. On closing day you sign the deed and settlement statement, the lender is paid off, and any rent or deposit for an occupied unit is credited to the right party.

Frequently asked questions

Do I register my DeKalb rental before selling it?

Registration is a duty while you own and lease the unit under Chapter 10. Ask the Crime Free Housing Bureau whether yours is current and what a buyer who keeps tenants must file afterward.

Where does a DeKalb deed get recorded?

The DeKalb County Clerk and Recorder, 110 East Sycamore Street in Sycamore, second floor. Title firms may file electronically, and paper filings remain accepted.

How much is transfer tax in DeKalb County?

It is 50 cents per $500 of value for the State plus 25 cents per $500 for the County. Filing happens through MyDec, and your closing agent buys the stamps.

When are DeKalb County tax bills due?

Near June 1 and September 1 each year. Late payments add 1.5 percent each month.

Can I sell a DeKalb rental with tenants inside?

Often yes, since investors buy occupied rentals. Hand over the lease, deposit records and contact details, and ask your closing agent how the deposit and current rent will be credited.

Belleville housing for a seller

Belleville is the St. Clair County seat in the Metro East, and its housing stock reflects almost two centuries of building. The first homes were simple brick cottages that locals called German street houses or row houses, and later decades added Foursquare, Italianate, Queen Anne and Victorian styles. A seller with a pre-war house here is often selling a property that has had many owners, many repairs and several rounds of wiring and plumbing updates.

Belleville has three locally designated historic districts: Old Belleville (1974), Hexenbuckel (1991) and Oakland (1995). A separate National Register district, listed in 1976, has 73 contributing properties. If your house sits inside one of them, ask the city's building staff what rules apply to exterior work before you sign a repair-heavy contract with a buyer.

Population and home values

The 2025 estimate for Belleville is 40,237 people, a 5.0 percent decline from the 42,358 in the 2020 base. With fewer people competing for the same stock, conventional buyers can take longer, so pricing matters.

Belleville housing and household figures
Housing figureBelleville
Typical home value (owner-occupied, 2020-2024)$141,300
Owner-occupied housing rate60.1%
Median gross rent$1,019
Households17,646
Median household income$63,535
Mean commute to work25.1 minutes

Values near $141,300 and rents near $1,019 put a premium on condition. The next two sections cover the city rules that can hold up a closing for owner-occupants and landlords alike.

Inspection and occupancy permit when a house sells

Belleville requires a Residential Certificate of Occupancy before a residence can be legally occupied, and the city's Health, Housing and Building Department issues it after an inspection of the dwelling. Sellers should call for a housing inspection as soon as they decide to sell, because a passed inspection can shorten the closing timeline and help the new owner get the occupancy permit.

  • The inspection covers electrical and plumbing systems, exterior and interior structure and other readily visible areas, checked against the city's housing code.
  • Defects must be corrected before occupancy is allowed, and a failed inspection means no permit until the violations are cleared and a reinspection is done.
  • All sewer bills for the property must be paid and current before an inspection can be scheduled or a permit issued.
  • The permit for a new occupant carries a $55 fee, and rental inspections cost $65 per dwelling unit.
  • The number of people allowed in a unit depends on bedroom square footage, so check the allowed count before finalizing a sales contract.

The department is at 2300 West Main Street, Building M, Suite M113, and takes calls at 618-233-6817 (option 1 for inspections). The counter is open weekdays from 8 in the morning to 5 in the evening. Those fee figures date from a June 2022 revision, so ask the department for current amounts. Any new occupant still needs the permit after a renovation, which is worth raising when you compare offers.

Rules for rental houses

Belleville has run a Crime Free Housing program since November 1, 2013, and any owner who leases a unit must register it. Registration costs $30 per dwelling unit, with renewals due by October 31 each year and fees doubling when a renewal is late.

Owners and managers must also complete the Crime Free Housing class, which the city now offers online, then email the department for a certificate. A leased unit needs a passed inspection, a nationwide background check on the tenant, the crime-free lease addendum and a signed lease before the tenant can obtain an occupancy permit. With a tenant in place, gather the registration receipt, the last passed inspection report and the lease so a buyer's lender or inspector can see the paperwork is in order.

A second failed reinspection carries a $50 fee. Vacant, tired rentals that would need work to pass are a common reason owners look at an as-is sale instead of fixing everything first.

Schools and commuting

Buyers ask about commutes and schools first, so have the facts ready.

  • High schools: Belleville Township High School District 201 runs Belleville East and Belleville West. Althoff Catholic High School is the Diocese of Belleville option, and parts of the city fall in East St. Louis District 189, Mascoutah District 19 and Freeburg District 77.
  • Grade schools: Districts 118, 119 (Belle Valley), 175 (Harmony Emge), 181 (Signal Hill), 115 (Whiteside) and 70 (Freeburg) all serve parts of Belleville, so the district depends on the street.
  • Transit and roads: Three St. Louis MetroLink stations sit in the city (Memorial Hospital, Belleville and College), and Illinois routes 15, 158, 159, 177, 13 and 161 pass through. Interstates 64 and 255 are adjacent.

Recording the deed in St. Clair County

Belleville deeds are filed at the St. Clair County Recorder of Deeds, whose office is at the county building on Public Square. The fee table for deeds received after July 1, 2023 lists $55.00 with the Rental Housing Support Program fee and $36.00 without it, with transfer tax added when applicable. The office takes cash, check or money order payable to Recorder of Deeds. Mail goes to PO Box 543, Belleville, IL 62222, and overnight carriers use 10 Public Square, 5th Floor.

Buyer and seller also complete the state's PTAX-203 transfer declaration, which goes to the county office. Counties may levy a 25-cent-per-$500 transfer tax and home rule municipalities may add another, so ask your closing agent which charges attach to a Belleville address. The Illinois Department of Revenue's Tax Rate Database has the rates.

Sellers who hold title through an estate or a family transfer should confirm the deed type with the title company before the closing date, since an exempt transfer is recorded differently from a sale.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Belleville houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment and pay taxes

Property in St. Clair County is reassessed every four years, and any change must be published in a county newspaper and mailed to the owner. If you think your value is out of line with neighbors, the first step is an informal review with the County Assessor's office. Most cases end there, but you can also file an appeal for a hearing before the Board of Review. Bring an exterior photo of your house and photos of at least three similar nearby properties, property record cards, or a recent appraisal, contract, settlement statement or deed. Evidence must reach the Board at least five days before the hearing or the assessment stands unchanged.

The Treasurer sends bills to the owner even when a lender escrows the taxes, and the owner stays responsible for penalties and interest. Unpaid taxes can lead the county to sell a lien. A principal dwelling with no more than six units can be redeemed for two and one-half years, and other property for two years. The Treasurer also runs a monthly payment plan for homeowners with the Homeowner Occupied Exemption, and online card payments carry a 2.5 percent convenience charge. Before closing, get this year's installment dates and a payoff figure from the Treasurer's office.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a Belleville house with failed occupancy inspection items?

Yes, but the new occupant cannot get a Residential Occupancy Permit until the violations are corrected and the unit passes reinspection. Ask the Health, Housing and Building Department for the written inspection report, then decide whether to repair, credit the buyer or sell to someone who plans the work.

Who records the deed after a Belleville sale?

The St. Clair County Recorder of Deeds files it, at $55.00 with the Rental Housing Support Program fee or $36.00 without, plus transfer tax when it applies. Your title company or attorney normally handles the filing.

Do Belleville landlords have to register rentals before selling?

Yes, while the unit is leased. Each leased dwelling unit must be registered and updated by October 31 every year. Keep the registration, inspection report and lease together so the buyer can see the unit was compliant.

What if my Belleville assessment looks too high?

Start with an informal review at the County Assessor's office, then file with the Board of Review if needed. Submit comparables or an appraisal at least five days before your hearing, because late evidence leaves the assessment unchanged.

Does the falling population affect my Belleville sale price?

The 2025 estimate of 40,237 is 5.0 percent under the 2020 base of 42,358. At a typical value near $141,300, condition and price both matter, so get two or three offers or a local agent's opinion before choosing a route.

Selling fast in Oswego

A direct cash sale gives the shortest wait before closing. A listing takes longer and rewards a house that shows well. Selling on your own is the third route, and it suits owners who have the time and a good title company.

Oswego is a village on the Fox River in Kendall County, with a small part in Will County. It is the largest municipality in Kendall County, with 39,948 residents, up 15.4% from 34,585 in 2020. Most of the housing went up in the building boom that began in the mid-1980s and pushed the village west of the river, so buyers tend to ask about roofs, windows and mechanical systems first.

  • Hire an agent if the roof, windows and mechanical systems are in good order and you can handle showings and a financing timeline.
  • Handle the sale yourself if you can price the home from recent nearby sales and coordinate the paperwork the village requires.
  • Take a cash buyer if the house needs work, is vacant, or belongs to an estate. Weigh the offer against a listing price after commission, repairs and the months of taxes and utilities you would carry.

A cash buyer takes the house as it is, so you skip the repair list that usually follows a buyer's inspection, and you skip the wait for a lender's appraisal and approval.

The Oswego transfer stamp

Oswego voters approved a real estate transfer tax on June 28, 2022. The buyer pays it at $3 per $1,000 of the sale price. A stamp from the village is required before the deed can be recorded with Kendall or Will County, even when the buyer is exempt from the tax.

The seller still has a part in the process, because open village bills block the stamp. Here is the sequence:

  1. The buyer or a representative sends a MyDec or PTAX-203 declaration at least three business days before closing, online or at Village Hall.
  2. The village prepares a Statement of Open Accounts. Any open invoice tied to the property must be paid in full before the stamp is released.
  3. After review, the buyer brings the deed to Village Hall at 100 Parkers Mill, open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m., and the tax is calculated while they wait.
  4. Payment is accepted by credit card, cash or certified check.

A person who has owned a primary residence in Oswego for at least a year is exempt when buying another Oswego home, but still obtains a stamp. The money goes to the water and sewer fund, tied to the Lake Michigan water connection through the DuPage Water Commission. Questions go to TransferTax@oswegoil.org or (630) 554-0864.

As the seller, check your water and sewer account early and pay anything outstanding. A small unpaid invoice is the most common thing that can hold up a stamp and push back the closing date.

How are Kendall County property taxes billed?

Kendall County mails one bill a year and collects it in two installments, in June and September. A late payment is charged 1.5% of the installment per month. Call the Collector for the exact dates on your bill.

The Collector's office is at 504 S. Main Street in Yorkville, open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., with the telephone at 630-553-4124. The county will not take estimated or partial payments, so the exact amount on the bill is required. It accepts payment online, by phone, by ACH, by mail, at most Kendall County banks, and in person, and a drop box outside the office is available at any hour.

Get a copy of the bill from the Collector. At the closing table, the title company splits that year's tax between you and the buyer by the days each of you owned the house, so you want the real figure in hand ahead of time. If your house is in the part of Oswego that lies in Will County, the bill comes from that county instead.

Permits and floodplain rules

Oswego handles residential permits through its Building and Permits department, and a long list of projects needs one. The village's application list covers basement remodels, decks, driveways, fences, fireplaces, garages, hot tubs, HVAC, irrigation systems, patios, pergolas, permanent pools, sheds, solar, sump pumps and downspouts, and window and door replacement.

Roof, siding, radon and water heater permits go through an online portal called Civic Access. The other applications are emailed to the department. If you did work on the house, gather the permit and final inspection records for the buyer, since a roof or window replacement with no permit on file is the sort of gap an inspector asks about, and a missing record can stall a closing that is otherwise ready.

Floodplain rules apply along the river and creeks. Any change to a structure in the floodplain may need a permit, and the substantial improvement rule generally limits an addition to less than fifty percent of the structure's value. The village has a floodplain map where you can check an address, and it asks owners to contact it before designing a project.

Which school district is your house in?

Oswego Community Unit School District 308 serves most of the village, and portions of Oswego fall within Yorkville Community Unit School District 115. Because District 308 also reaches Boulder Hill, Montgomery, Plainfield, Aurora, Yorkville and Joliet, the attendance zone is not always obvious from the village name. Confirm the district for your address before listing, and name the nearest elementary and junior high on the flyer.

The closing for an Oswego sale follows a plain order. The buyer's side files the declaration, the village reports any open accounts, you pay what is owed, the village releases the stamp, and the deed goes to the county for recording. Nothing in that order needs the house to be repaired, which is one reason owners with a vacant or inherited property choose a cash buyer who can work around the village's timing.

A short list of what to have ready when you sell: the tax bill, permit and inspection records for any work, receipts for sump pump or drainage work, and the water and sewer account number.

Oswego housing numbers

Owners live in 87.9% of Oswego homes, so most sales are owner to owner, and typical buyers are families who will want a clean inspection.

Frequently asked questions

Who pays the Oswego real estate transfer tax?

The buyer. The tax is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, and a village stamp is needed before the deed is recorded. The seller's part is clearing any open village invoices on the property.

How early must the transfer declaration reach Oswego?

At least three business days before closing. Send a MyDec or PTAX-203 to the village online or at Village Hall, and the village will then prepare its Statement of Open Accounts.

Is anyone exempt from the Oswego transfer tax?

Yes. Owners of an Oswego primary residence for at least one year are exempt when they buy another home in the village, though they still need a stamp.

When are Kendall County property taxes due?

Kendall County issues one bill, payable in two parts in June and September, and charges 1.5% per month on late payments. Call the Collector at 630-553-4124 for the dates on your bill.

Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Oswego?

Yes. Roof permits are filed through the village's Civic Access online portal. Keep the permit and final inspection record to hand to the buyer.

Selling an Urbana house: your options

Listing through an agent, selling alone and accepting a cash buyer's as-is price all work in Urbana. Tenants change the picture, because the city runs a rental registration program, and the University of Illinois next door keeps the rental market busy.

Urbana sits in Champaign County, shares its western edge with the city of Champaign, and holds most of the university campus. Population was 38,336 at the 2020 count and is estimated at 39,719 for mid-2025.

Urbana housing market

This is a young, renter-heavy city where home values sit far under those in the Chicago suburbs. Only 37.3% of homes are lived in by their owners: there are 10,569 renter-occupied units against 6,287 owner-occupied ones, across 16,856 households.

The middle value of an owned home is $184,900, and the middle rent with utilities is $972 a month. Median household income is $45,346. Median age is 27.2, and 72.8% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. If you own a house here, your likely buyers are other owners, investors and families tied to the university.

Rental registration and inspection

The city has more than 10,000 rental units, nearly two-thirds of its housing, and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign enrolls more than 50,000 students annually. The city runs a Rental Registration and Inspection Program, described on its program page.

  • Every rental property must register each year and pay a fee from the city's schedule of fees.
  • The program year runs from October 15 to October 14, matching the leasing calendar.
  • It covers single-family homes, duplexes and multi-family buildings, including room rentals where the owner also lives there.
  • Nursing homes, hotels and motels, housing authority units and university-certified housing are excluded.
  • The city aims to inspect every rental on a cycle of three to five years, and results appear in its open data portal.

Landlords register through an online Citizenserve account, and the Building Safety Division answers questions at 217-384-2443. If you own a rental, make sure the registration is current before you list, and ask the division what the inspection record shows.

Property tax bills and due dates

The Champaign County Treasurer and Collector bills and collects the tax from the Bennett Administrative Center at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana, phone 217-384-3743. The county mails one bill for the full year with coupons for two equal installments, and no second bill follows. The office handles more than 77,000 real estate bills for 156 taxing districts, including school districts, cities and villages.

December 1 to 31Advance payments accepted, from 50% of the prior year's total up to 10% over it

Postmarks do not count for the late-payment dates, so pay early. If the county has an old mailing address for you, call the Supervisor of Assessments at 217-384-3760.

Exemptions and tax programs

The Treasurer's tax page lists the programs and the office that handles each one. Most go through the County Assessment Office at 217-384-3760, which is also the number for corrections to bill information.

  • Owner-occupied exemption
  • Over-65 exemption for real estate, and the Senior Assessment Freeze
  • Disabled persons exemption and various exemptions for military service
  • Natural disaster homestead exemption
  • Tax deferral for owners over 65, run by the County Treasurer

Before you sell, ask the assessment office what is on file for the parcel, so the buyer's first bill is not a surprise.

Selling with back taxes

Champaign County has elected to act as trustee for the taxing districts on delinquent real estate taxes, beginning with the 2025 taxes payable in 2026 (Public Act 104-0553). At the delinquent sale, the county takes the taxes in place of private tax buyers.

If back taxes are owed, get a payoff from the Treasurer before a closing date is fixed. The title search will surface the balance regardless, and it gets paid from your sale money at the table. Learn the number now and every offer can be weighed against what lands in your pocket.
