Most construction, remodeling and improvement projects need a permit before work starts, and permits can help prevent issues in later property sales. For inspections, call the Building Division at 847-599-7550 with 24 hours' notice and your permit number.

The Village sets a maximum U-factor of 0.28 for replacement windows in residential projects, so keep the contractor's paperwork if you replaced yours. Water arrives from Lake Michigan through the Central Lake County Joint Action Water Agency. The Village website has a Start, Stop or Make Changes page for your service, which is the place to end your account near the closing date.

The Lake County Clerk's recording division in Waukegan takes the deed. A PTAX-203 declaration or a signed exemption statement is also required.

Six municipalities require a local stamp before recording: Buffalo Grove, Highland Park, Lake Forest, Lincolnshire, Mettawa and North Chicago. Gurnee is not one of them, but a quick call to the Village before closing settles it.

Before the transfer stamp is issued

Call the Finance Department at 847-588-8030 ten days before closing. The village uses that call to arrange a final water reading and a property search for fines, fees or violations.

  • Buy stamps in person at the Finance Department in Niles Village Hall, or by mail to 1000 Civic Center Drive with a self-addressed, postage-paid envelope.
  • In-person transactions must reach the Finance Department before 4:30 pm with paperwork already complete.
  • Payment can be a cashier's check, money order, title company check, attorney firm check, cash, or a credit or debit card with a processing fee.
  • Completed forms can be emailed to the village's real estate transfer stamp address, with the property address in the subject line. Water reading and property search requests must be phoned in, not emailed.

A lien, an unpaid water bill or an open code violation will stop the stamp, so get the property search result early enough to fix anything that turns up.

Selling a Niles rental

If the transfer declarations show the new owner will not live there, the buyer must file a Rental License Application when buying the transfer stamp. Rental licenses are non-transferable when a property is sold, so the license you hold does not pass to the buyer.

That affects a landlord selling to another investor and a family selling a house that will be rented out. Questions about the application go to Community Development at 847-588-8040. If you have a tenant in place, check the lease and ask the buyer's side how it plans to apply for the license.

Transfer tax rebate for Niles residents who buy again

A narrow group qualifies. A Niles resident who sold a principal residence and buys a residential structure in the village to use as a principal residence can claim a rebate of $2 per $1,000, equal to two-thirds of the amount paid for the transfer stamp on the new property.

The buyer files after closing, with proof of the transaction, within one year of the sale of the old residence. The Finance Director reviews the claim, and commercial and retail property do not qualify. If you are moving up or down within Niles, keep the closing statements from both deals.

Schools and transit

Several elementary districts cover the village: East Maine District 63, Park Ridge-Niles District 64, Golf District 67, Niles District 71 and Fairview District 72. High school students attend Maine Township District 207 or Niles Township Community District 219. Confirm the district for your address before you list.

Niles runs a free village bus, and Pace operates its Pulse Milwaukee and Pulse Dempster lines through town. U.S. 14 and Illinois routes 21, 43 and 58 cross the village, and Golf Mill Shopping Center is a long-standing retail anchor.

Household makeup

Median gross rent is $1,336. The village has 11,481 households averaging 2.51 people, and the median household income is $75,274. Of residents age 5 and older, 59.5% speak a language other than English at home, so listing materials in more than one language can reach more buyers.

Steps from contract to closing

Plan the Niles part of a sale around the stamp. First, sign the contract and agree on who pays each layer: the buyer pays the village stamp, and the seller is liable for the state and county charges. Second, call Finance ten days before closing for the water reading and property search. Third, clear any lien, unpaid bill or open violation the search finds, because the stamp waits on that.

Fourth, complete the Niles Real Estate Transfer Declaration Form along with the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, and get the paperwork to Village Hall before 4:30 pm if you are delivering it. Finally, if the buyer will rent the house out, make sure the Rental License Application goes in with the stamp request.

A cash buyer can often close on a short timeline, but the ten-day village call and the property search still apply, so build that lead time into any quick closing.

What to gather for the Niles stamp

Put a small folder together before you call Finance. It should hold the signed contract, the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, the completed Niles Real Estate Transfer Declaration Form, the property address and parcel number, and a payment method the village accepts. Title companies and attorneys often handle this step, so ask yours whether it will request the water reading and property search or whether you must phone them in yourself.

If the deed is not a sale, such as adding or removing a name, ask for the exempt stamp. It costs a flat $25.00, but the property still has to be clear of fines and fees first. Questions about open violations go to Community Development at 847-588-8040.

Finally, remember that email is fine for completed forms but not for the water reading or property search. Those need a phone call, and the ten-day clock starts when you make it.

Frequently asked questions

Who pays the Niles real estate transfer tax?

The buyer pays the village stamp, at $3.00 per $1,000 of price or fraction thereof. The state ($.50 per $500) and the county ($.25 per $500) are the seller's responsibility.

How early should I call the village before closing on a Niles house?

Ten days before closing. The Finance Department asks the seller to call 847-588-8030 so it can take a final water reading and run a property search for fines, fees and violations.

Can a Niles stamp be issued with an unpaid water bill or violation on the property?

No. The property must be free of liens and violations and cannot have outstanding bills owed to the village. Exempt stamps are also held until all fines and fees are paid.

What does a Niles buyer need if the house will be a rental?

A Rental License Application, filed at the time the transfer stamp is bought. Rental licenses do not carry over to the buyer when a property is sold.

Does Niles refund any of the transfer tax?

Only to a Niles resident who sold a principal residence and buys another residence in the village, and only on a form filed within one year. The rebate is $2 per $1,000, calculated as two-thirds of the stamp price paid on the new property.

How a McHenry homeowner goes about selling

Three paths are open. An agent can list the house, you can find a buyer yourself, or you can deal with a purchaser who accepts the house as it sits and brings no lender. Once a contract exists, every path ends at the same county filing: a transfer declaration plus a recorded deed.

Condition and calendar settle the choice. Patience plus a tidy interior favors open houses. Worn systems, a tenant, an estate in limbo or a hard closing date tilt toward a direct purchase.

What follows sticks to McHenry itself: housing figures, the permit rules at 333 S Green Street, how city water accounts change hands, and what the county recorder expects.

McHenry at a glance

The city is in east-central McHenry County, about 55 miles from the Chicago Loop and 35 from O'Hare, over about 13 square miles of land, and is organized around two state routes, 31 and 120. By the 1920s the Fox River and nearby lakes had made the town a summer destination, and summer cottages spread along the river. Subdivisions were annexed on every side from the late 1940s onward, such as Boone Creek, Glacier Ridge, Legend Lakes, Liberty Trails and Prairie Lakes.

Population was 27,135 in 2020 and is estimated at 29,217 for mid-2025, up 6.8 percent. Owners live in 74.4 percent of the 11,897 households. A typical owned home is valued at $266,500, median rent runs $1,553, and household income sits at $86,315 (all figures 2020 to 2024). Roughly three in four homes are owner-occupied, so the people you compete with are mostly neighbors. Getting to work takes 29.0 minutes on average.

Schools, roads and rail

McHenry Community High School District 156 and McHenry School District 15 (five elementary and three middle schools) both serve the city.

  • Roads: Route 31 and Route 120 cross in the middle of town and carry most traffic in and out.
  • Rail: the city is the last stop on a Metra branch that offers weekday trains into downtown Chicago.
  • Trails and parks: the Prairie Trail runs through the center, while Moraine Hills State Park, anchored by 48-acre Lake Defiance, lies on the east side.
  • Airports: O'Hare and Milwaukee Mitchell are the closest public international airports.

Downtown is split into Green Street, Riverside Drive and Main Street, tied together by a 0.73 mile Riverwalk along Boone Creek and the Fox River.

Winter, water and drainage

Expect scrutiny of the roof, gutters, attic insulation, furnace and basement. The area sees about 34.5 inches of snow a year, and yearly precipitation totals close to 37 inches, peaking in May and June, so a basement that smells damp or a sump pump that cycles constantly will show up on an inspection.

Glacial lakes, Boone Creek and the Fox River give the area its character and also its drainage questions. If the lot lies near the water, find out its flood zone designation before you name a price.

Permits when a McHenry house is on the market

Most remodeling and home improvement jobs in McHenry need a building permit. Sort out any open or missing permits early. The Community Development Department answers at 815-363-2170 and sits in the Municipal Center, 333 S Green Street.

Most residential permit applications are processed within 10 business days, and the clock does not start until everything needed for review has been submitted. Some permits are issued faster:

  • Reroof, siding, and windows or doors.
  • Water heater and furnace or air conditioner replacement.
  • Sewer or water repair.

Those counter-based permits come back immediately for walk-in applicants and within a day for online ones. The permit fee already covers the inspections, which need a day's notice and are booked in three-hour windows (9 to noon or 1 to 4, except roofing and siding, which run 10 to 2). Same-day inspections are not offered.

If an earlier owner skipped paperwork on a deck or basement, the department can say what finishing it involves. Investors often absorb that cost; buyers with mortgages tend to raise it.

Where a McHenry deed goes after closing

The county Recorder's Office handles it, not city hall. A document that meets state formatting rules and comes with the right payment is recorded the same day, then mailed back in roughly two working days. For fees, ring 815-334-4110.

Sale prices are visible through a PTAX-203 or MyDec form that can accompany the deed. The state levy is set in 35 ILCS 200/31-15 at fifty cents for every $500 of value, with revenue stamps as proof. No McHenry County municipality adds its own transfer tax. For ownership by parcel number, the Assessor's number is 815-334-4290; for tax bills, the County Treasurer's is 815-334-4072.

What a McHenry seller owes the buyer and the city utility

Under 765 ILCS 77/20 the seller fills out every item of the statutory report and puts it in the buyer's hands before anyone signs a contract. Finish it while offers are still coming in.

City water and sewer bills arrive every two months, and accounts fall on even or odd billing months depending on the account number prefix. McHenry publishes a Water/Sewer Transfer Form that records the ownership date along with billing addresses for the outgoing and incoming owner. Submitting it fixes the date your final bill stops.

The title company will ask for a loan payoff figure if you owe on the house, along with the parcel number and your latest tax bill. Put the transfer form, the disclosure report, the permit history and those papers in one folder, so a buyer or title officer gets answers in a single request. Call the County Treasurer at 815-334-4072 if you are unsure whether a tax bill is paid.

Which McHenry selling route fits which situation?

Set the three paths side by side before choosing.

  • Agent listing: the largest audience, in return for showings, an appraisal and inspection, and possible repair requests from the buyer.
  • Owner-handled sale: control over price and timing, with the paperwork and promotion landing on you.
  • Direct sale for cash: quicker, with fewer conditions, and priced around the repairs ahead.

With any offer, insist on a written copy and read each closing cost line.

Frequently asked questions

Do roof and water heater swaps in McHenry need city sign-off?

Yes. Both jobs sit on the city's counter-based permit list, which means same-visit approval in person or a one-day turnaround online. Community Development at 815-363-2170 can say what your project requires.

Is there a McHenry city transfer stamp?

No. None of the county's municipalities levy their own, so the state's fifty cents on each $500 (35 ILCS 200/31-15) is the charge.

Who records the McHenry deed?

The McHenry County Recorder, at 815-334-4110. Documents that conform and carry the right payment are recorded the day they arrive.

How does the city water account change hands?

McHenry bills every second month and provides a Water/Sewer Transfer Form noting the ownership date. File it at closing and each owner pays only for their own period.

Will anyone buy a McHenry house that needs work?

Yes. Illinois asks only that the disclosure report precede the contract; fixes are bargained over afterward. Mortgage-backed buyers lean on repair requests, while investors price the work into their offer.

Roads and access

Illinois Route 47 is the main north-south road and runs nearly seven miles through the village. It was widened from two to five lanes in 2011, carries over 20,000 vehicles a day, and meets I-90 at a full interchange finished in November 2013. Algonquin Road runs east toward Algonquin and Lake in the Hills, and Main Street connects west toward Marengo and Harmony Road. Huntley-Dundee Road leads east to the Carpentersville and Dundee area.

Mean commute is 29.5 minutes. A listing can point to the I-90 and Route 47 access as a practical selling point.

A cash buyer does not need a mortgage, so the sale does not wait on a lender's appraisal or a loan approval. That matters most for the sellers Huntley has plenty of: people settling an estate, moving closer to family, or leaving a rental they no longer want to manage.

Selling in New Lenox

New Lenox is a village in central Will County, about 36 miles southwest of downtown Chicago. Population is 28,893 (July 1, 2025 estimate). Owners live in 92.4% of homes, the middle home value is $399,900, and households average 3.05 people, so these are mostly family-sized houses.

Commutes average 32.7 minutes, which is why the Metra station and the I-80 and I-355 ramps are the first things a commuting buyer looks up.

Village permits and open permit work

Most construction and homeowner projects need a village permit, including sheds, decks, pools, fences, roofs, lawn irrigation, siding, window replacement, room additions and basement remodels. Homeowners may do the work themselves, but any contractor must be registered with the Village before the permit is issued.

  • The minimum building permit fee is $75.00. Fees for garages, remodeling, room additions and in-ground pools depend on project cost.
  • Small jobs such as fences, sheds, driveways, roofs and windows can be reviewed over the counter and issued the same day if the application is accurate. Larger reviews can take up to two weeks.
  • Online applications are accepted for furnaces, water heaters, air conditioners, demolition, driveways, electrical upgrades, fences, generators, irrigation systems, roofs, rooftop solar, sewer repairs, and window, door and siding replacement.
  • Online applicants should hear a status within two business days, and no work may begin until the permit is paid for and issued.

Private sidewalks, concrete or paver patios, dog runs and playhouses under 100 square feet do not need one. Community Development answers questions at 815-462-6490, and Village Hall takes in-person applications from 8:30 am to 5 pm on weekdays.

Inspections and winter concrete rules

If a permit was never closed out, the Village's inspection steps apply. It asks for 48 hours of notice for building inspections and 24 hours for water meter and plumbing inspections, and it charges a fee for a failed inspection, including one where the work is not ready when the inspector arrives.

Winter adds a second limit. From December 1 through March 30 the Village prohibits placing concrete flatwork, and it regulates timing and insulation for footings and foundations. Bonds are accepted in place of exterior concrete during those months. If you have an unfinished driveway apron or public walk, ask the Building Department how the bond works before a closing date is set.

The Village also keeps a Vacant Property Registration form on its permits page. If the house will sit empty during a sale, ask Community Development whether that registration applies to you.

Recording a deed with Will County

New Lenox deeds record with the Will County Recorder of Deeds at 158 N. Scott Street in Joliet, phone 815-740-4637. The fee schedule effective October 1, 2025 lists $90.00 for a standard document and $118.00 for a non-standard one, and the $19.00 Rental Housing Support Program surcharge is part of those totals.

The recorder's deed checklist asks for:

  • The preparer's name and mailing address, and a return address for the document.
  • The permanent index number and a legal description.
  • A notarized original deed, not a copy.
  • The grantee name and address, and the name and address for tax bills.
  • A completed transfer declaration or exemption under the Illinois transfer tax law.

The checklist also names nine municipalities whose transfer stamps must be on a deed: Aurora, Bolingbrook, Channahon, Joliet, Naperville, Park Forest, Romeoville, University Park and Woodridge. Lincoln-Way Central and Lincoln-Way West are in New Lenox, and Providence Catholic High School is also in the village.

U.S. Route 30 is the main east-west road, with Cedar, Gougar and Nelson roads running north and south. I-80 and I-355 both pass through. The Metra Rock Island District station is at U.S. 30 and Cedar Road, and a second station at Laraway Road is on the SouthWest Service line.

Winter wear on a house

January averages about 21 degrees Fahrenheit and July averages 73, with 137 days a year at or below freezing. Those swings are hard on roofs, gutters, driveways and basement sump systems. Keep receipts for roof work and the sump pump, since both come up in nearly every sale.

Parks buyers ask about

The New Lenox Community Park District maintains 40 parks and athletic fields on nearly 600 acres. The 22-mile Old Plank Road Trail passes through the village, and Hickory Creek State Nature Preserve and Hadley Valley Preserve add more trail miles. A house near the trail or a park is worth a line in the listing.

Steps to a closing

A sale here goes in a straight line. Start by checking permits for any deck, roof, finished basement or addition, and call Community Development at 815-462-6490 if a record is missing. Next, settle the contract terms, including whether the buyer takes the house in its present condition and who handles any unfinished exterior concrete.

Then prepare the deed to the recorder's checklist: original notarized signature, legal description, permanent index number, and the transfer declaration or exemption. Ask Village Hall whether any payoff or final billing step applies. A cash buyer can usually work to your date and skip the repair negotiation, which helps a seller with unpermitted work or a roof near the end of its life.

Keep your closing statement and the recorded deed together afterward. If a permit question comes up later, those papers show what was done and when.

What to have on hand for the buyer's review

Buyers and their inspectors tend to ask the same few questions about a house here. Have answers ready for the roof, the sump pump, the furnace and any deck, shed or finished basement. For each, a permit number or a contractor receipt is the best proof. If something was done without a permit, say so plainly and let the buyer decide how to handle it, or sell to a cash buyer who takes the house as it stands.

Also gather your most recent water bill, the parcel number and your loan payoff details. Having them in one folder shortens the time between accepting an offer and setting a closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a village permit before selling my New Lenox house?

Not to sell, but open permits and unpermitted work can come up in a buyer's review. The Village requires permits for most construction projects, so call Community Development at 815-462-6490 if you remodeled, added a deck or replaced a roof.

Which office records a New Lenox deed?

The Will County Recorder of Deeds in Joliet. The standard document fee is $90.00 since October 1, 2025, and the deed must be an original with a notarized signature, a legal description and a permanent index number.

Does New Lenox charge a municipal transfer tax stamp?

The Will County deed checklist names nine municipalities that issue transfer stamps, and New Lenox is not among them. Ask Community Development at 815-462-6490 before closing to confirm.

Can I sell a New Lenox house with unfinished concrete work?

Yes, but winter timing matters. The Village bars concrete flatwork from December 1 through March 30 and accepts a bond in place of exterior concrete during that period, so ask the Building Department what the bond requires.

How old are most New Lenox houses?

Most of the building came between 1990 and 2010. The count rose from 9,627 in 1990 to 17,771 in 2000 and 24,394 in 2010, so houses from those years are common.

Quickest ways to sell in Glen Ellyn

Speed in Glen Ellyn usually comes from an as-is purchase by a buyer with no loan to approve, although a well-prepared listing can also hit a fixed date. What slows most closings is the village paperwork: the transfer stamp, the clearwater inspection and the final water reading.

  • An agent listing suits a house in good shape when you want to see how high the price can go.
  • Sell privately if you are comfortable handling contracts and disclosures on your own.
  • A cash purchase as-is fits a house with deferred repairs, an estate behind it, or a closing date that cannot move.

Glen Ellyn is a village in DuPage County about 24 miles due west of downtown Chicago, in Milton Township. Train access, school boundaries and basement drainage are the topics to prepare before you talk to buyers.

Glen Ellyn housing snapshot

Glen Ellyn is a high-value suburb where most residents own. Population is 28,750, and the village has 10,698 households.

Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $544,000, and owners hold 78.3 percent of the housing. Median gross rent is $1,433 and median household income is $140,938.

The average trip to work takes 29.1 minutes, which is worth reading alongside the train and expressway access described below. Much of the housing is older, since the village dates to the 1800s and the railroad reached it in 1849.

Schools, trains and parks

School district is the first fact to confirm for any Glen Ellyn address. Primary schools are part of Glen Ellyn School District 41 and Community Consolidated School District 89, and high school students attend Glenbard Township High School District 87.

Elementary schools in the village include Abraham Lincoln, Arbor View, Benjamin Franklin, Churchill, Forest Glen, Park View and Westfield, and Glen Crest Middle School and Hadley Junior High serve older grades. Confirm which school serves your address with the district, since district boundaries do not follow village lines everywhere.

The Metra Union Pacific West Line stops at the Glen Ellyn station at 551 Crescent Boulevard, about 22.4 miles from Ogilvie Transportation Center. Pace routes 714, 715 and 301 run along Roosevelt Road, and Roosevelt Road also leads to Interstate 355 at the east end of the village. The Glen Ellyn Park District maintains 30 parks and two lakes, and the Illinois Prairie Path bike trail runs through the village.

Transfer stamp and clearwater inspection

The Village of Glen Ellyn charges a real estate transfer stamp of $3 for each $1,000 of property sales price, and the home seller pays it. The stamp is required to record the deed, and the village will not issue it until every inspection is passed and every fee is paid.

Steps before a Glen Ellyn transfer stamp is issued
StepWho handles itContact
Transfer stamp application, completed onlineVillage of Glen EllynOnline form
Clearwater inspectionPublic Works630-469-6756, choose clearwater appointments
Final water readingUtility Billing630-547-5235
Stamp tax of $3 per $1,000 of sales pricePaid by the sellerVillage

The clearwater inspection comes from Village Code 3-42-15. It is required any time a stamp is needed, including a sale, a title transfer, putting a deed into a trust or a refinance, and it applies to exempt transactions too. The inspector checks whether the building has a sump pump and whether the pump is illegally tied into the sanitary sewer.

Why the village checks sump pumps

Rainwater in the sanitary system can overload it during a major storm and push sewage back into homes. Village Code 7-9-25 bars clearwater from sanitary sewers, and Code 8-1-10 bars directing sump pump, gutter or similar discharge into the public right-of-way.

If the inspector finds a problem, fix it before closing. Public Works can explain acceptable options, which may include moving the discharge point or connecting to the storm sewer. Book the inspection early, since a failed result means a repair and a second visit before the stamp can be issued.

Some sellers may qualify for a refund of the transfer tax. The eligibility rules are on the village's refund application, so ask the village before assuming one applies.

Permits and contractor rules

Permit work in Glen Ellyn goes through the village's online permit system, and open work can complicate a sale. The Building Division reviews plans, issues permits, inspects construction and enforces the building, property maintenance, fire and zoning codes.

Applications are signed electronically with the owner's authorization, and supporting documents such as plans, a plat of survey and contracts are uploaded with them. Construction plans must be prepared and stamped by an Illinois registered design professional. Fees depend on the project type and construction cost, and refundable deposits cover possible damage to public property. All contractors must meet the license and insurance requirements in Village Code Section 4-1-11, and a contractor working in violation can be cited or have a stop work order issued.

  • Locate permit records and final inspection sign-offs for decks, additions and finished basements.
  • Ask Public Works about drainage if your lot has a history of standing water.
  • Keep a copy of your plat of survey, since many permit and closing steps ask for it.

Selling as-is to a cash buyer puts the cleanup of open permits on the buyer, as long as the contract spells out who takes on what.

DuPage County property taxes

Glen Ellyn sits in Milton Township, and DuPage County sends a single yearly bill with two coupons. They come due June 1 and September 1, and the U.S. postmark decides whether a payment is late. Late payments add 1.5 percent a month.

Valuation questions start at the township assessor, who sets the first assessed value at one-third of fair market value under state law. An owner who disagrees files with the DuPage County Board of Review within 30 days after the township roll is published, backed by three or more comparable properties. Decisions typically arrive the next March, and the next level is the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

New owners should contact the township assessor after moving in, because the residential exemption requires that you live in the home by January 1 of the tax year. For parcel questions, call the DuPage Supervisor of Assessments at 630-407-5858 or the Treasurer at 630-407-5900. Your closing agent prorates the bill at settlement, so ask the title company how the current year is being split.

Frequently asked questions

Who pays the Glen Ellyn transfer stamp?

The home seller pays it. The rate is $3 for each $1,000 of sales price, and the stamp is issued only after the clearwater inspection is passed and all fees are paid.

What is a clearwater inspection in Glen Ellyn?

It is a village check for a sump pump and for any illegal sump connection to the sanitary sewer. Village Code 3-42-15 requires it when a transfer stamp is needed, and you schedule it with Public Works at 630-469-6756.

How do I schedule the final water reading in Glen Ellyn?

Call the Utility Billing Department at 630-547-5235 after you complete the online transfer stamp application. The reading and the clearwater inspection both come before the stamp.

Can I sell my Glen Ellyn house without making repairs?

Yes, apart from anything required for the stamp, such as correcting an illegal clearwater connection. Cosmetic and mechanical repairs are negotiable in an as-is sale and are priced into the offer.

When are DuPage County property taxes due?

In two installments, June 1 and September 1. The coupons on your bill show the exact dates each year, and late payments add 1.5 percent a month.

How selling a house in Lake in the Hills works

Three paths are open to an owner: hire an agent, handle the sale yourself, or sign with an investor who pays cash and skips the repair list. Whichever route you pick, a sale runs through the same local pieces: Village Hall for permits and contractor questions, the three fire protection districts and four school districts that overlap the village, and the McHenry County Recorder for the deed.

Lake in the Hills sits in McHenry County, northwest of Chicago, along the Randall Road corridor. The 2020 census counted 28,982 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 28,590. A seller here is usually working with a house built after the 1990s growth wave, or with an older lakeside cottage on the east side of the village, and the two behave very differently at sale time.

Neighborhoods buyers compare

The village began as a summer-cottage community around Woods Creek Lake, formed on November 29, 1952, and became a commuter suburb. Growth exploded in the 1990s, when roughly 17,000 people were added and the village issued more than 1,000 residential building permits in 1995 alone.

Randall Road now splits the village into an older East Side and a newer West Side, and Algonquin Road marks the boundary with the village of Algonquin. Buyers tend to compare houses by subdivision, so it helps to know which one yours belongs to.

  • The Old Section: four older neighborhoods (Original, Indian, Tree and Presidents, named for their street themes) near the lake, with mixed architecture instead of tract styling.
  • Boulder Ridge: a gated community north of Algonquin Road with the village's only 18-hole golf course.
  • Big Sky and Harvest Gate: early subdivisions west of Randall Road, split by Woods Creek and close to the village hall and Lincoln Prairie Elementary.
  • Spring Lake Farm: an early-1990s subdivision south of Miller Road with both single-family and multifamily housing.

School and fire districts by address

Four school districts share the village, so the district tied to your street matters to many buyers. Consolidated District 158 covers most of the dense western half, District 300 covers the older eastern sections, and Elementary District 47 and Community High School District 155 reach a small central slice.

A seller on the west side may market Huntley High School, while a seller on the east side points to Jacobs High School in Algonquin, and the central pocket feeds Crystal Lake South and Crystal Lake Central.

Fire service is also split. Three separate districts, the Algonquin-Lake in the Hills Fire Protection District, Crystal Lake Fire Rescue and the Huntley Fire Protection District, serve different parts of town, each with its own taxing authority. Check your tax bill or call the district before you describe the house in a listing.

With nearly three people per household and more than a quarter of residents under 18, three- and four-bedroom floor plans are the common fit. Interstate 90 is about seven miles south, a drive most commuters make along Randall Road.

Permits before you list

No permit is needed just to sell, but any construction, remodeling that changes structure, plumbing, electrical or heating, and many replacements need one first. Village Hall at 600 Harvest Gate reviews both zoning and building code before a permit issues, at 847-960-7400.

  • Applications can be emailed as PDFs to the community development address, dropped in the box at the Village Hall parking lot entrance, or brought in person.
  • Air conditioners, furnaces, roofing, siding, water heaters and water softeners can be permitted through the online portal.
  • Contractors need village credentials, so call Village Hall to confirm a name before hiring.
  • Plumbing inspections are offered Monday, Tuesday and Thursday from noon to 4 p.m.
  • Village approval does not depend on your homeowner association, so check the association separately.

If a past owner finished a basement or deck and you cannot find the permit, ask Village Hall what is on file for the address before a buyer's inspector asks. A buyer paying cash for the house as-is may accept that risk, but a lender-backed buyer often will not.

Snow, trash and noise rules

Winter and noise rules are the ones sellers trip over. The village plows most streets, aims to clear them 6 to 10 hours after snow stops, and bans on-street parking once an inch has fallen under Municipal Code Section 41.03. County crews handle roads such as Algonquin, Lakewood, Randall and Ackman, and the state handles Routes 31 and 47.

Property owners clear their own sidewalks and driveways, and snow belongs in the yard, not the street. Garbage cans go to the curb at 6 p.m. or later the evening before pickup and should be stored out of sight otherwise. Construction, lawn work and personal snow removal are exempt from the noise limits only between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m., which matters if you are rushing repairs before listing.

Recording and transfer in McHenry County

Deeds are filed with the McHenry County Recorder, and the state transfer tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 is fifty cents per $500 increment of the value written on the declaration. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-25 the paperwork is due with the deed or inside three business days of the transfer, whichever comes first, with a seller's and a buyer's signature (or those of their agents).

Check these items before closing:

  • The online MyDec declaration must read "Closing Completed."
  • A deed needs the grantee's address and the full McHenry County legal description.
  • A Plat Act affidavit must accompany a deed that uses a metes and bounds description.
  • A signed exemption paragraph or a PTAX-203 or MyDec declaration must come with every deed.
  • Documents need a half-inch clean margin and a clear 3 by 5 inch space in the upper right corner.

Call the McHenry County Recorder to ask whether a county or village transfer fee applies to your parcel.

When a cash offer fits

A cash sale makes sense when the house needs work a lender's appraiser would flag, when you inherited a home you cannot maintain, or when the calendar matters more than squeezing out the top price. Houses with deferred maintenance, an association dispute or a pending violation notice are typical examples, since each can slow a conventional listing.

Compare any offer against a listing by asking the buyer to state the closing date, who pays recording and transfer charges, and whether repairs are priced in. Get that in writing, then confirm the title company will handle the PTAX declaration and the recorder submission.

A cash sale also skips the loan approval wait, so the deed paperwork above is usually the only schedule that matters.

What if my Lake in the Hills house has open permits?

Expect the buyer or title company to ask about them. Contact Village Hall at 600 Harvest Gate to see what is open for the address, then either finish the inspections or disclose the work. A cash buyer may take the house with the open item priced in.

Which office records my deed?

The McHenry County Recorder records deeds for Lake in the Hills. A deed needs a completed transfer declaration, the grantee's address and the full legal description, and the MyDec record must show that closing was completed.

Do homeowner associations affect permits here?

Village approval is based on codes and zoning, not on your association. Many subdivisions still have their own rules, so get any needed association sign-off in addition to the village permit.

Who handles snow removal on my street?

It depends on the road. The village clears most local streets, county crews handle Algonquin, Lakewood, Randall and Ackman Roads, the state handles Routes 31 and 47, and some roads belong to property owner associations. Call 847-960-7500 for a specific street.

How is the state transfer tax stated?

It is set in 35 ILCS 200/31-10 and applies to the value shown on the declaration. A deed that says it conveys the property subject to a mortgage lets the unpaid mortgage balance be left out of the base.

Routes to a fast sale in Galesburg

Your options in Galesburg: hire an agent, handle the sale personally, or hand the keys to a buyer who accepts the place with every flaw. The right choice follows from the shape of the house and how firm your closing date is. Prices in the city run low, so repair bills weigh heavily against the sale price.

  • Agent listing: a good match for a house in decent condition when you can sit through showings and loan approvals.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you skip the agent fee and take over the pricing, contract and paperwork.
  • As-is offer: suits inherited houses, empty properties, rentals with tenant trouble and homes with repairs put off for years.

The city is the seat of Knox County, about 45 miles northwest of Peoria. That puts the county Treasurer and assessment office, the two county offices that touch every sale, within a short drive of any Galesburg address.

Galesburg housing market

Galesburg is inexpensive and getting smaller. Population is 28,581, down 4.9 percent from 30,046 in the 2020 base. In the 2020 census, 10.9 percent of Galesburg's 13,939 housing units were vacant.

Across 12,628 households, owners live in 62.2 percent of the housing, and the middle value of those homes is $96,400 in the 2020 to 2024 figures. Rent has a median of $801 and household income a median of $48,297. Low prices and short commutes, averaging 16.6 minutes, draw first-time buyers and small investors, so price a Galesburg house against recent Galesburg sales rather than suburban figures.

A 496-acre area is designated as the Galesburg Historic District on the National Register, which matters if your house lies in or beside it.

Roads, rail and neighborhoods

Location in Galesburg is mostly about access and the age of the housing stock. Interstate 74 runs along the east side of the city, leading southeast to Peoria and north toward the Quad Cities. US 34 is a freeway through Galesburg with interchanges at West Main Street, North Henderson Street and North Seminary Street, and US 150 enters as Grand Avenue and runs through downtown as Main Street.

Amtrak offers four daily trains to Chicago Union Station, and Galesburg Transit operates four bus loops. A home near the rail corridor will hear freight traffic, since BNSF runs a large hump yard south of town and its lines through the area carry an average of about seven freight trains per hour. Be upfront about that when you show a house nearby.

Ask the local school district for the attendance area of your address so buyers get the same answer you do.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Galesburg house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Weather and housing age: what buyers inspect

Buyers in Galesburg look hard at roofs, furnaces and basements, because the weather is rough on all three. January lows average close to 14 degrees, and a typical year brings about 26 inches of snow and 39 inches of precipitation.

With so many older houses, certain items come up again and again in inspections and lender reviews:

  • Roof age and flashing after years of freezing and thawing.
  • The age of the furnace and water heater, and working carbon monoxide detectors.
  • Basement moisture and the condition of the sump pump.
  • Outdated panels or early wiring in houses from the early 1900s.

If a repair costs more than it would add to the sale price, an as-is buyer can carry it. If you list instead, an inspection done before you list removes surprises that might otherwise sink an offer.

Permits and city rules

Call the City of Galesburg Inspection Division at 309-345-3619 before starting any project, since talking with an inspector first is the best way to learn whether a permit is needed. Residential building, fence, swimming pool, demolition, sign, roofing, electrical, plumbing and HVAC applications can be submitted through the city's online portal.

A homeowner may do general construction, electrical, plumbing and heating work on their own residence without a contractor license or bond, as long as the correct permits are pulled and occupancy is proven. Contract work is different: general contractors must register with the City Clerk for $125 per calendar year, and electrical contractors must pass testing, hold a license and be bonded. On the code side, Galesburg enforces the 2021 editions of the international building, residential, mechanical, fuel gas, existing building and fire codes.

The Property Compliance Division also enforces nuisance rules. Complaints it handles include grass or weeds over 12 inches, inoperable vehicles, trash and debris, dangerous structures, outside storage, front yard parking and pests. Violation notices go to both the owner and the occupant, and unresolved cases can bring fees, fines and court action. Settle any open violation notice ahead of closing, because it follows the property.

Selling a rental house

A Galesburg landlord must secure a rental license from the City Clerk each year for every property, and the license must be in place before the unit is leased.

Galesburg and Knox County rental and tax costs
ChargeAmount or date
Rental license$25 per unit per year; apply May 1 to May 31 for the next year
Late rental licenseExtra $10 per unit after May 31
General contractor registration$125 for the calendar year
Knox County tax installmentsJuly 1 and September 1

Every rental falls under self-inspection, city inspection or noncompliant city inspection. All new rentals need a city inspection before a tenant moves in, and any unit can be inspected after a complaint. A landlord with unpaid fines or fees at the city cannot get a rental license. If a tenant lives there, pass along the newest inspection report and name the inspection category your unit is in.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Galesburg houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Knox County property taxes

The county mails one bill per year, with two stubs attached. The stubs are due July 1 and September 1, and lateness costs 1.5 percent a month. Make checks payable to the Knox County Collector, pay at a county bank other than Wells Fargo, or use a card, which carries a fee of 2.35 percent or $2.95 at minimum.

Appeals go to the Board of Review, which sets a filing window each fall, so call ahead for the dates. A Board of Review ruling can go further to the state Property Tax Appeal Board, within 30 days. The question in an appeal is the value of the property, never the size of the bill.

The basic homestead exemption belongs to owners who live in the house on January 1. New owners should phone the assessment office after closing and confirm the parcel shows it. The assessment office also runs the senior exemptions, whose freeze program caps household income at $75,000 for 2026, plus programs for improvements and disabled owners. Applications are requested by September 30 and accepted through December 31. Reach the Treasurer at 309-343-3121 and the assessment office at 309-345-3845.

Frequently asked questions

Is a vacant or run-down Galesburg house still sellable?

Yes. Vacant and worn houses change hands as-is all the time, usually at a price that reflects the work. Clear any open nuisance notice first, such as grass over 12 inches or debris, so the city does not hold up the sale.

Will the city inspect a Galesburg house before I sell?

Rentals must pass a city inspection before a tenant moves in, and any unit can be inspected after a complaint. The Inspection Division, at 309-345-3619, can tell you whether any inspection applies to your address.

How much does a Galesburg rental license cost?

It is $25 per rental unit per year, with applications accepted May 1 through May 31. After May 31 a $10 per unit late fee applies, and the fee is waived for fully sprinklered units with hard-wired detectors.

When do Knox County property taxes come due?

July 1 and September 1. The bill itself shows the dates each year. The late penalty is 1.5 percent a month and is not prorated.

Which office answers property tax questions for a Galesburg home?

Start with the Knox County Treasurer for payments and the county assessment office for exemptions and values. Appeals are heard by the Board of Review.

How a house changes hands in Burbank

Most Burbank houses sell by listing, by a private deal between neighbors or relatives, or to an investor who pays cash. Residents here tend to stay: 80.9 percent of homes are occupied by their owners, and 92.9 percent of residents had not moved in the past year.

That low turnover shapes a sale. Long-time owners often put off a new roof, a furnace or rewiring, so a buyer's inspector may produce a long list. A seller facing that list can fix items before listing, offer a credit, or hand the house to a buyer who expects to do the work. Whichever path you take, the City Clerk and the Cook County recording office are on the route to closing.

Burbank housing numbers

Burbank is a Cook County city in Stickney Township, ZIP code 60459. The latest population estimate is 28,578, which is 3.0 percent below the 2020 base. The typical home value is $275,700 for 2020 through 2024 across 9,539 households, typical gross rent is $1,265, middle household income is $80,116, and the one-way commute is 31.3 minutes.

Most of the area was built out after 1950, so a typical house is now about seven decades old. Buyers' first questions concern roofs, furnaces and plumbing. Pace buses link the city with the southwest side of Chicago and the south suburbs.

Transfer tax at the City Clerk

Burbank taxes the transfer of a house. The City Clerk's page posts a two-part transfer tax form, refreshed in 2024, and the office at 6530 W 79th Street processes it. Phone 708-599-5500 before closing to confirm the rate, who pays and which transfers are exempt.

The clerk works weekdays, closing at 5 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday and at 6 p.m. on Tuesday. The office is closed on weekends. The city posts its 2026 closure dates, which include the Friday after Thanksgiving, so plan the stamp pickup around them.

The state's separate levy is collected through the county recorder, and the Illinois Department of Revenue's PTAX-203 declaration goes in with the deed at recording.

Repairs that need a city permit

The Building Department at City Hall decides whether a project needs a permit. It calls for one on new construction and on structural, ventilation, exit, plumbing, electrical and fire-safety changes. The city's page lists many everyday jobs.

  • Roof recoating or replacement, siding, gutters and masonry.
  • Fences, driveways, porches, sheds and garages.
  • Furnaces, air conditioning and boilers.
  • Any remodel, plus demolition of a structure.

Every contractor who works in Burbank has to meet the city's contractor requirements, and swapping a gas water heater earns a no-charge inspection of venting, safety valve and connections. The office answers at 708-599-5500, option 2.

A buyer's attorney will ask whether past work was permitted. An unpermitted change can slow a conventional sale, which is why some owners choose a buyer who accepts the house with those questions open.

Paperwork to line up before closing

The title company or attorney usually runs the process, but only you can supply the permit history and confirm who owns the property of record.

Burbank seller paperwork
DocumentWhere it comes from
DeedYour records, so the clerk and recorder can match the owners

Exemptions show up as deductions on the second installment bill. If you cannot tell whether a homeowner or senior exemption is in place, ask the Assessor or the Treasurer before closing, because it shifts the proration on the settlement statement.

The recording office run by the Cook County Clerk keeps hours of 9 to 5, accepts its last customer at 4:45 and offers a legal help desk staffed by volunteer attorneys.

Open violations and code questions

The Building Commissioner's office handles permit reviews, property maintenance and code enforcement, along with variance and zoning requests. Call 708-599-5500, option 2, with questions about your address, and ask for the permit and violation history in writing if you can.

If your house has an open violation, resolve it before the contract is signed. A title search or a buyer's inspection can surface it, and an unresolved item can stall a closing or cost you leverage in a price talk.

Clearing out the house

Emptying a house after an inheritance or a move often starts with a sale of the contents, and Burbank regulates those. Garage sales need a permit from the Building Department, are barred on Sundays and are capped at two per year. Guidelines and fees are available at 708-599-5500, option 2.

Plan the cleanout dates with that cap in mind, since an owner who held two sales earlier in the year cannot hold a third. Anything left over can go with a hauler before the final walkthrough. If the house is going to a cash buyer who accepts it with contents in place, ask for that in the contract so nobody has to haul anything.

Marketing to Burbank buyers

Of residents, 51.1 percent are Hispanic or Latino, and 60.9 percent of residents age 5 and over speak another language at home. A listing with Spanish-language materials, or a translator at showings, reaches households a one-language flyer would miss.

The mix includes young families and long-settled older owners. Yard and school access speak to the first group, and single-floor living and easy maintenance speak to the second.

From accepted offer to closing

A Burbank sale usually runs in this order. Your title company or attorney opens the file and orders the title search. You and the buyer sign the PTAX-203. Someone picks up the city transfer tax form from the clerk's page and brings it to the office with the deed, after a phone call to confirm the rate and who pays. The Cook County Clerk records the deed, and the state's levy is collected at that step.

Call the Building Department before you list if you remember work on the roof, furnace or plumbing. Finding out about an unclosed permit in week one of a contract is much worse than finding out in week one of your listing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What a cash sale skips

A cash buyer does not wait on a lender's appraisal or underwriting, so the closing date is easier to hold. The clerk's transfer form, the PTAX-203 and the recording step still apply, and so does the question of open permits. Compare offers by what you net after repairs, not by the headline number.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I find Burbank transfer tax forms?

On the City Clerk's page at burbankil.gov, where the two-page form was updated in 2024, or at the clerk's office, 6530 W 79th Street. Call 708-599-5500 to confirm what to bring.

When is the Burbank clerk's office open?

Weekdays, with Tuesday running to 6 p.m. and the other weekdays closing at 5 p.m. The office is shut on weekends and on the closure dates the city posts.

Which county records a Burbank deed?

Cook County, through its Clerk's recording office, which takes customers from 9 a.m. until 4:45 p.m.

Is a permit required for re-roofing in Burbank?

Yes. The Building Department names roof replacement among the work that needs a permit. Phone 708-599-5500, option 2, to confirm the steps for your address.

Can a Burbank house with repair problems be sold?

Yes. Cash buyers routinely take houses in their present state. Collect permit records, ask the Building Department about anything open, and compare offers by what you net after repairs.

The Danville housing market for a seller

Danville is an affordable, slower-moving market where repair costs can rival a house's value. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $79,000. The city is the seat of Vermilion County, with 28,138 residents, down from 33,027 in 2010. Owner-occupied homes make up 57.3 percent of housing, median gross rent is $846, and there are 11,901 households of about 2.19 people.

Many Danville sellers are heirs, landlords with aging rentals, or owners of houses that have sat empty. When a roof or furnace costs a large share of what the house would sell for, an as-is sale deserves a serious look next to a listing.

Danville's vacant building ordinance

If the house is empty, Danville's Chapter 169 can add registration fees that must be settled before the house changes hands. The owner of a vacant building must register with the Public Development Department within 30 days after the building becomes vacant.

Danville vacant building rules that matter at closing
RuleWhat the ordinance requires
Who must registerThe owner, within 30 days after the building becomes vacant
Residential registration fee$50 (non-residential is $100)
Annual fee if the building stays vacant$500, held in abeyance while permitted repairs make progress
Fees at transferPaid by the owner before any transfer, and disclosed by the seller to the buyer
If unpaid at transferNew owner pays the annual fee plus $300 within 30 days
Penalty for violations$250 to $2,500 per offense, with each day counted separately

A new owner must also re-register a vacant building within 30 days of any transfer and follow the plan the previous owner filed until changes are approved. A building counts as vacant when it is unoccupied and, for example, unsecured, unsafe, under an order to correct violations or illegally occupied. Ask the Public Development Department whether your property is on the registry before you sign a contract.

If the house is vacant and you plan to sell soon, a practical order is: confirm the registry status, pay any fee that is owed, get a payoff letter for any lender, and tell the buyer in writing about every fee on the property. A cash buyer will usually ask about this up front, and having the answer ready keeps the closing date from slipping. If repairs are underway under a permit, mention that too, since the annual fee is held in abeyance while permitted work makes progress.

Utilities, code enforcement and rentals

Utility accounts and code enforcement are the two other places the city touches a sale. The utility billing office is at 17 W Main Street. Bring a signed and dated copy of the deed so the account can be prorated, because accounts are billed by date of ownership, not occupancy.

  • Account name: residential accounts must be in the owner's name, and a landlord's bill stays in the landlord's name.
  • Flat fees: every property owner pays flat sewer and solid waste fees regardless of usage, so a vacant house still gets a bill.
  • Due dates: accounts beginning with 08 are due on the 8th of each month and those beginning with 04 on the 20th, adjusted when the date falls on a weekend.
  • Rental registration: all rental units and vacant structures must be registered and a fee paid each year.

Common code violations include grass over six inches, trash in the yard, inoperable vehicles, missing house numbers and toters left out too long. Clearing those cheaply before showings makes the house look cared for and avoids a notice during the sale.

Recording a Danville deed

Deeds for Danville property go to the Vermilion County Recorder at 201 N Vermilion Street, Danville, Illinois 61832. The office phone is (217) 554-6040, and it accepts documents by mail if you include a check for the exact fee and a self-addressed return envelope.

Every sale or gift needs a newly prepared, signed, notarized and recorded deed. When the sale involves consideration above $100, Illinois Form PTAX-203 must be completed and submitted with the deed. The form collects the state and county transfer taxes, which are based on the sale price. A gift is exempt from those taxes, but the deed must carry the right exemption statement. The state rate, set in 35 ILCS 200/31-10, is 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500.

Recorder staff cannot offer legal advice, run title searches or refer you to an attorney, so line those up yourself. A copy of a recorded deed costs $1.00 per page, and a deed presented in person is usually returned within five minutes of scanning. For current recording fees, call the office, because the schedule is revised from time to time. Questions about back taxes go to the County Treasurer, and parcel details to the Supervisor of Assessments.

Selling an inherited or estate house

If the house came to you from an estate, ask an attorney whether title is clear before accepting any offer. Gather the recorded deed, the latest tax bill and the utility account details. Because every sale or gift needs a newly prepared deed, the names on the new deed must match the people who actually hold title. Buyers who pay cash generally still require clean title, so sort out any missing signatures before you pick a closing date.

Cash buyer or listing in Danville

Set the numbers side by side and include the costs that never appear in an offer. A house valued near the city median of $79,000 can leave little room for repairs, agent fees and months of carrying costs, so a quick as-is closing can be worth more than it first appears.

  • Get written repair bids for the roof, furnace, plumbing and electrical items an inspector would flag.
  • Check whether the building is registered as vacant and whether any fees are owed.
  • Ask for the closing date and confirm who pays recording and title charges.
  • Compare the figure against a listing agent's price opinion for the same house.

Illinois law requires you to deliver a residential disclosure report before the contract is signed under 765 ILCS 77/20, even when you sell as-is.

On closing day expect to sign the deed before a notary, sign the PTAX-203 declaration, and receive a settlement statement showing payoffs and prorated charges. Call the utility billing office with the deed copy the same week so the final bill is cut on the right date, and keep proof that any vacant building or rental registration fee was paid.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a vacant house in Danville?

Yes. If the house is registered as vacant, the city ordinance requires the fees to be paid before transfer and disclosed to the buyer. An unpaid annual fee passes to the new owner with an extra $300.

Where do I record the deed for a Danville sale?

Take or mail it to the Vermilion County Recorder at 201 N Vermilion Street in Danville. A sale above $100 also needs Illinois Form PTAX-203 filed with the deed.

How do I transfer utilities when my Danville house sells?

Bring a signed and dated copy of the deed to the utility billing office at 17 W Main Street or email it. The city prorates the account by date of ownership.

Do I owe a transfer tax to the city of Danville?

State and county transfer taxes are collected through the PTAX-203 form. Ask the title company to confirm the exact charges that apply to your sale.

Do I have to register my Danville rental before selling it?

Rental units must be registered and a fee paid each year. Contact the code enforcement office to confirm the registration is current before you sell.

Your options for selling a house in Lansing

A Lansing owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or take a cash offer for the house as-is. Lansing is a Cook County village on the Indiana line, so a sale involves three layers of paperwork: the village for its seller certificate, the Cook County Clerk for recording and county transfer tax, and the State of Illinois for the transfer declaration.

Lansing is a home rule community, which gives the village more room than most to write its own local rules. That is why the village's own requirements get most of the space below.

Location and housing stock

Lansing sits 6.9 miles south of the Chicago city limits at 138th Street and about 25.6 miles from the Loop. Its neighbors are South Holland and Calumet City to the north, Thornton and Glenwood to the west, Lynwood to the south, and Munster and Hammond in Indiana to the east. The 2020 census counted 29,076 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 28,068.

The first settler family arrived in 1843 and the village incorporated in 1893. Buyers often like an established village, so a seller can mention that long local history.

Transportation options include Pace bus service, the Grand Trunk Western Main Line between Chicago and Port Huron, and the South Shore Line station at Munster Ridge in Indiana, which opened to riders on March 31, 2026. Most commuters still drive.

Lansing housing figures

Housing here is affordable, and a median owner-occupied value of $177,000 is a useful anchor when you price. Figures below are 2020 to 2024 estimates.

Schools

Two elementary districts and one high school district serve the village. District 158 runs Coolidge, Lester Crawl, Oak Glen and Reavis schools plus Memorial Junior High for grades 6 to 8. Sunnybrook District 171 runs Nathan Hale for PreK through grade 4 and Heritage Middle School for grades 5 to 8. Thornton Fractional South High School in District 215 takes students for grades 9 to 12.

Private and parochial options include St. Ann, Lansing Christian, Trinity Lutheran, Saint John Lutheran and Eagle Christian Academy. Buyers with children usually start by asking which of the two elementary districts covers a given address, so have the answer ready.

What Lansing requires when a house changes hands

The village, not the county, attaches its own condition to the sale. Lansing's rule, enacted May 21, 2013, makes the seller liable, and a certificate of payment from the village must be attached to the recording. There is no fee exemption.

  • Call the Lansing Municipal Center at 3141 Ridge Road, 708-895-7200, to learn how to obtain the certificate before the closing date.
  • Confirm the final stamp amount with the village before closing.
  • The state tax is 50 cents per $500 and the county tax is 25 cents per $500, with the seller named as the liable party for both.

Build the certificate into your closing timeline. A missing certificate can hold up the buyer's possession.

Water, vacancies and permits

Residential water service needs a deposit of $100, paid at the Municipal Center after possession, with a driver's license and the closing documents. If a property has sat vacant four months or longer, the Building Commissioner must inspect it before that deposit is taken.

That last rule matters if you are selling a vacant or inherited house. Expect the buyer to need an inspection before water can be turned on, and consider scheduling it yourself so the sale is not held up.

  • Permits: the Building Department handles permits, contractor licenses and property maintenance, at (708) 895-7193. Four property maintenance inspectors investigate complaints and issue violation notices.
  • Vehicle stickers: new residents have 30 days to buy village stickers, and you must bring a closing document or lease.
  • Trash: each single-family home gets three toters, and yard waste collection runs April 1 through November 30.

A folder for the buyer

A few small items fit in a folder you can hand over at closing. Vehicle stickers go on sale May 1 each year and expire June 30, and a buyer who moves in mid-year has 30 days to buy one. Dog and cat tags are required annually and go on sale in mid-May at the Municipal Center.

Garbage and recycling use village-issued toters that stay with the house, and leaves go in the green-lidded toter or brown paper bags from April 1 through November 30. Tree trimming is the property owner's job. For utilities, buyers call ComEd for electricity and Nicor Gas for gas. Leaving the toters, the service numbers and any pet or sticker records for the buyer shortens the first week after closing.

Does flooding affect selling a house in Lansing?

It can. The village keeps a flood information section covering the Little Calumet River, flood hazard, flood proofing and protection regulations, and it links to resources for Cook County residents affected by the storms and flooding of August 16 to 19, 2025. If your lot is near the river or has a history of basement water, gather any repair receipts and elevation or insurance paperwork before you list.

FEMA publishes the official flood maps at its Map Service Center, and the village can point you to its own guidance. A buyer's insurance quote often decides whether a deal closes, so being open about past water problems protects the sale.

When is a cash offer a reasonable choice in Lansing?

With a median owner-occupied value of $177,000, a large repair bill takes a bigger share of the price. If the roof, sewer line or basement needs work and you would rather not manage contractors, a cash buyer who takes the house as-is removes that step. Ask for a closing date in writing, ask who pays for the seller certificate, and confirm the buyer's title company will submit the transfer declaration.

A cash sale also skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, so the village certificate is usually the item to schedule first. Keep a copy of the certificate and your closing documents, since you will need them again if a title question comes up later.

Who pays transfer tax when selling in Lansing?

The seller is liable for the state tax, the Cook County tax and Lansing's own certificate of payment. Confirm final amounts with the village before closing.

Do I need an inspection before the buyer gets water?

Only if the property has been vacant four months or more. In that case the Building Commissioner must inspect before the $100 water deposit is accepted. An occupied house goes straight to deposit and application at the Municipal Center.

Which office handles permits in Lansing?

The Building Department at the Lansing Municipal Center handles permits and contractor licenses. Call (708) 895-7193 before starting any home improvement. Most improvements need a permit.

Which high school serves Lansing?

Thornton Fractional South High School, part of District 215, serves the village. Elementary students attend either District 158 or Sunnybrook District 171 depending on the address.

Is Lansing in a flood-prone area?

Parts of the area sit near the Little Calumet River, and the village publishes flood hazard and protection information. Check the FEMA flood map for your parcel and ask your insurer before listing.

Lockport owners can list through an agent, sell by owner, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases the house in its current condition. One local detail simplifies the money side: Lockport does not impose a city transfer tax, so the taxes at closing come from the state and the county.

Lockport is in Will County, so the deed goes to the Will County Recorder of Deeds in Joliet, and property tax questions go to the Will County Treasurer and Supervisor of Assessments.

Lockport at a glance

Lockport sits on the east bank of the Des Plaines River just north of Joliet, with the village of Lemont about two miles north. Population was 26,094 in the 2020 census and is estimated at 27,822 for July 2025, up 6.6 percent from the 2020 base.

The city grew around the Illinois and Michigan Canal, and canal-era buildings remain, including the Gaylord Building (1838, local limestone) and the Norton Building (1850). The city also has a Historic Preservation District with its own permit rules, which affects what an owner there can change.

Owners are the majority: 84.6 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the median value is $316,000, and median gross rent is $1,525. There are 9,903 households and median household income is $111,981. Commuters have alternatives to driving: Lockport has a Metra Heritage Corridor station with weekday rush-hour service to Chicago Union Station, Pace routes 832 and 834 reach Joliet, and Interstate 355 runs through the area. The mean travel time to work is 35.3 minutes.

Schools and districts

All of Lockport falls in Lockport Township High School District 205, whose Central Campus (opened 1910) serves freshmen and whose East Campus (opened 1964) serves sophomores through seniors. The grade-school pattern is more fragmented, and the district tied to a street can change a buyer's interest.

  • Taft School District 90 covers the southwest part of the city.
  • Milne-Kelvin Grove District 91 covers the west central part, with Milne Grove for kindergarten through grade 3 and Kelvin Grove for grades 4 to 8.
  • Will County School District 92 serves the north, with Walsh, Reed, Ludwig and Oak Prairie schools.
  • Homer District 33C serves the east and Fairmont District 89 serves the south.

Over-the-counter permits cover HVAC, water heaters, roofs, siding and windows, and other work goes through plan review that typically takes 10 to 14 business days when the submission is complete. A remodeling permit stays valid six months, and a new building permit one year.

  • Contractors working in the city must register with the Building Department before starting, and work hours are 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Saturday and 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday.
  • Owners may do their own work on an owner-occupied single-family home, but the city does not allow house flipping unless every tradesperson registers.
  • A swimming pool 24 inches or deeper needs a permit and a four-foot barrier with a self-closing, self-locking gate.
  • Changes inside the Historic District need a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Planning Department.

For the plat of survey, look in your closing papers first, since the city usually holds a plat only for homes built since 2002. A new survey costs about $500 by the city's estimate.

The landlord program

If the house has been rented, the Code Enforcement Department runs a landlord rental property registration with health and life safety inspections. Its duties also include abandoned vehicles, grass over 8 inches, exterior maintenance on dilapidated buildings, pool barrier violations and signs without permits.

An investor buying a Lockport rental should ask the department how the registration transfers, and a seller moving out of a former rental should ask whether the property is registered. Code Enforcement answers at 815-838-0549, extension 2153 for the assistant line.

Streets, parks and flood maps

Buyers ask who plows and repairs the street. The Illinois Department of Transportation maintains Route 7 (9th Street and 159th Street), Route 53 (Broadway), Route 171 (State Street and Archer Avenue) and New Avenue. Will County maintains roads such as 143rd Street, Briggs Street and Cedar Road, and the city maintains streets including Farrell Road and Division Street west of Briggs.

The Lockport Township Park District, created in 1945, manages 38 parks, and Dellwood Park hosts October haunted attractions. For flood risk, check FEMA's Flood Map Service Center and call the city Engineering Department, because a floodplain location can change building requirements and insurance needs. Pull the map for your parcel before you list. A private-line sewer or water repair stays with the owner, while main-line problems belong to the city.

Order a final water reading by calling the Water Department at 815-838-0549, option 3, with the closing date, a forwarding address for the final bill and the purchaser's name. Water and garbage bills mail around the first of the month and are due by the 15th.

Trash and recycling run through an inclusive city contract with Waste Management, with yard waste collected from April 1 through the first week of December. For winter, the city maintains 108 miles of roadway with 11 snowplow trucks and aims to clear streets within 24 hours after snow stops. Parking on city streets is banned when snowfall exceeds 2 inches, and curb parking is barred from 3 to 6 a.m. The city replaced vehicle stickers in 2015 with a municipal electric excise tax, so a buyer has no sticker to purchase.

On the private side, the homeowner owns the sewer line from the house to the main, and a home with a sprinkler system needs an annual backflow (RPZ) test report before the system is turned on each season.

Recording and taxes in Will County

Recording happens at the Will County Recorder of Deeds in Joliet, 815-740-4637. The Illinois transfer declaration and the 50-cent-per-$500 state tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 still apply even though Lockport adds nothing. Property tax bills come from the Will County Treasurer. Delinquent taxes can be sold at the annual tax sale, with homeowners typically getting one to three years to redeem. Call the treasurer about current balances before you set a closing date.

No. Lockport does not impose a transfer tax. The state tax of 50 cents per $500 under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 still applies to the sale.

Call the city Water Department at 815-838-0549, option 3, with the closing date, the address for the final bill and the purchaser's name. Bills mail around the first of the month and are due by the 15th.

Can I do my own repairs before selling?

Yes, if you own and live in a single-family home, though permits are still required and the city bars house flipping unless all trades register. Painting, tuckpointing and fixture swaps need no permit outside the Historic District.

Which school district covers my Lockport address?

Every address is in Lockport Township High School District 205. Grade school depends on the street: Taft 90, Milne-Kelvin Grove 91, Will County 92, Homer 33C or Fairmont 89. Confirm with the district before listing.

Is a historic district permit different?

Yes. Changes within the Historic District go through the Certificate of Appropriateness process with the Planning Department, and the list of exempt ordinary repairs does not apply there.

How the occupancy permit works

Most vehicle complaints belong with the Police Department.

The department also issues certificates of occupancy for newly occupied units and runs property maintenance inspections, and the permit page links a certificate of occupancy checklist and a pre-inspection checklist. If you are unsure whether a past deck, fence or basement finish was permitted, ask the department before listing, because a buyer's title or lender review can raise the same question.

How the property tax bill is set and paid

Lake County sets Vernon Hills bills on a two-year cycle, so the bill you receive reflects an assessment made the year before. The county's Tax Extension Process page explains the steps: township assessors value each home as of January 1 at one-third of fair market value, the Chief County Assessor equalizes the values, and a blue assessment notice goes out in the fall. Owners then have only 30 days to appeal to the Board of Review. By the time the bill arrives it is too late to contest it.

Bills are mailed each May 1, with the first installment due in early June and the second in early September. Penalty interest of 1.5% is added the day after each due date, and more accrues in later months. A tax sale of delinquent parcels follows in November.

Taxes for the year in progress are usually adjusted between buyer and seller at closing, so get a paid-to-date figure from the Lake County Treasurer before the closing is scheduled.

Appealing an assessment before you sell

The blue assessment notice that arrives in the fall is your one chance each year to contest the value. Read it when it comes, compare it with what similar homes nearby have sold for, and decide quickly, since the window to file with the Board of Review is only 30 days.

A lower assessment helps whoever owns the house next, and buyers notice tax bills when they run their monthly numbers. If you plan to sell within the year, filing on time can make the property easier to market. Keep a copy of the notice and any evidence you send, and pass the paperwork to the buyer's side if the appeal is still open at closing.
